passages.title: The clear victory and its fourfold purpose
passages.tafsir:
Allah calls a peace treaty that had bitterly disappointed the Muslims **"a manifest victory"** — and then states what that victory was given *for*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts three bounties there: forgiveness, guidance to a straight path, and mighty support. Ayat 2 and 3 are not fresh announcements but the purpose-clause of ayah 1.

## The event behind the words: Hudaybiyah

Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agree — Maʿārif reporting it as the consensus of the Companions, the Tābiʿīn and the leading authorities on Qurʼanic commentary — that this sūrah was revealed as the Prophet ﷺ was returning from Hudaybiyah, in Dhul-Qaʿdah of the sixth year after the Hijrah.

The story begins with a dream. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports (from Ibn Jarīr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Bayhaqī and others) that in Madinah the Prophet ﷺ saw himself going to Makkah with his Companions, entering it peacefully and performing ʿumrah, after which they left the pilgrim-garb, some shaving their heads and others cutting their hair short; he then entered the House of Allah and its key fell into his hand. A prophet's dream is not a mere dream or fiction; it is divine revelation, and acting upon it is necessary. But no date was specified. The Companions, in their eagerness to visit Makkah and perform *ṭawāf*, began preparations at once, and the Prophet ﷺ made up his mind to accomplish the vision then.

He bathed, put on his new clothes and mounted his camel Qaṣwāʼ. According to most versions there were fourteen hundred people altogether, and they had no weapons except swords. At Dhul-Ḥulayfah he donned the pilgrim-garb — *iḥrām* — with the intention of ʿumrah. Some bedouin refused his invitation to join, claiming he wanted to push them into the jaws of death against Makkans superior in weapons and power.

Letting him enter would leave all Arabia under the impression that the Makkans had been subdued by him. Quraysh dispatched an advance cavalry under Khālid ibn al-Walīd — who until then was not a Muslim — to intercept him. When Khālid's horsemen watched the Muslims pray Ẓuhr in congregation, he said afterwards that they had lost a golden opportunity to wipe them out while they prayed, and that he would wait, since soon they would be praying again. But Jibrīl brought down the injunction of *ṣalāt al-khawf*, the prayer of fear, and the army prayed in two alternating groups, one praying while the other stood guard.

**The camel that would not rise.** Near Hudaybiyah, Qaṣwāʼ's forelegs slipped and she sat down; the Companions tried to urge her up, but in vain. They thought she was enraged. The Prophet ﷺ said it was no fault of hers, nor her usual habit, and that:

> "He Who stopped the elephant, has stopped her too."

Ibn Kathir records that he then declared, "By the Name of Him in Whose Hand my soul is, this day, if they ask me anything which will respect the ordinances of Allah, I will grant it to them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests what lay behind that sentence: that by then he had probably discerned that the time was not yet up for the fulfilment of his vision.

**Water from a dry well.** Al-Bukhārī records from al-Barāʼ ibn ʿĀzib that the Muslims drank Hudaybiyah's well dry. The Prophet ﷺ sat on the edge of the well, asked to be brought a bucket of water and used it for ablution, rinsed his mouth, invoked Allah and poured that water into the well — and soon it provided them and their animals with water in whatever amount they wished. Maʿārif adds a second miracle on the return journey at ʿUsfān: their provisions were depleted, the little each had was gathered on one dining-sheet, the Prophet ﷺ supplicated, and all fourteen hundred ate to the full, yet nothing had diminished.

**The pledge under the tree.** ʿUthmān was sent into Makkah as envoy. Imam Bayhaqī reports, on the authority of ʿUrwah ibn Zubayr, that the Prophet ﷺ first called upon ʿUmar for this task, but ʿUmar said Quraysh were his implacable enemy and that there was not a single member of his tribe in Makkah who would support him; he proposed ʿUthmān, who because of his tribe held special power and honour there. Offered the chance to perform ṭawāf himself, ʿUthmān refused: he would not do it unless the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had performed it first. Then a rumour reached the camp that he had been assassinated. The Prophet ﷺ gathered the Companions under an acacia tree and took a solemn pledge from them that they would fight Quraysh to the last breath of their lives. This is *bayʿat al-Riḍwān*, the pledge signifying that those who took it had obtained Allah's pleasure. Because ʿUthmān was away on the Prophet's ﷺ own errand, the Prophet ﷺ placed one of his own hands on the other and said, "This is ʿUthmān's pledge."

**The treaty.** Suhayl ibn ʿAmr objected to *bismillāhir-raḥmānir-raḥīm*, saying those words did not exist in their idiom; the Prophet ﷺ agreed to *bismika Allāhumma*. Suhayl objected to "Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah", arguing that they did not recognise him as such; the Prophet ﷺ granted this too and told ʿAlī to write "son of ʿAbdullāh" instead. ʿAlī, for all his obedience, said he could not erase the title, and Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr and Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah withheld his hand. So the Prophet ﷺ, who had never written before, took the document and wrote the preamble himself: war suspended for ten years, during which neither party would attack the other. The Muslims would retire that year and come back the next for three days only, carrying no arms but sheathed swords. And most painfully, at Suhayl's insistence: a Makkan who went over to the Muslims without his guardian's permission would be sent back, while any of the Prophet's ﷺ followers who went over to Quraysh would not be returned. Then Abū Jandal, Suhayl's own son, escaped to the camp — a Muslim whom his father had imprisoned and persecuted harshly, fetters about his ankles and signs of violence on his body. The Prophet ﷺ, already bound by the treaty, asked him to be patient a little while longer, for soon Allah would pave the way for him and the other helpless Muslims detained in Makkah.

**ʿUmar's questions.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān preserves the exchange. "O Messenger of Allah! are you not the True Prophet of Allah?" He replied: "Why not!" "Are we not on the right path and they on the wrong?" — "Why not!" "Is it not a fact that our martyrs are in the Paradise and their slain ones in the Fire?" — "Why not!" Then: "Why should we submit to this humiliation and return without observing ʿUmrah or Allah decides the matter through war?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ replied: "I am the servant of Allah and His Messenger. I can never violate His command. He will never destroy me. He is my Helper." And when ʿUmar asked whether he had not promised them that they would visit Allah's House and perform ṭawāf, he answered: "Yes, indeed, I did promise, but did I promise that it will happen this year?" ʿUmar put the same questions to Abū Bakr, and heard the same counsel: hold on to his stirrup until the last breath of your life; by Allah, he is on the path of truth. ʿUmar is reported to have said, as transmitted by Bukhārī, "I never gave way to doubt since I embraced Islam, but on this occasion I could not avoid it." Abū ʿUbaydah suggested he seek refuge with Allah from the evils of Shayṭān, and he did. He says that since he realised those misgivings he continued to observe voluntary prayers, keep voluntary fasts, emancipate slaves and give alms, so that Allah might pardon his error.

When the Prophet ﷺ told them to slaughter their sacrificial animals in that very place, shave their heads and put off the pilgrim-garb, no one moved, so overwhelmed were they with grief. It was Umm Salamah who gave the most apt advice: do not reprimand them now, for they are acutely grieved; call the barber in the presence of all, shave your own head, put off your own pilgrim-garb and slaughter your own camel. He followed her advice — and when the Companions saw it, they followed suit.

## Why a treaty is called *fatḥ*

It was on the way back, at Kurāʿ al-Ghamīm, that Sūrah al-Fatḥ was revealed, and the Prophet ﷺ recited it to the Companions. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that ʿUmar could hardly contain himself and inquired: "Messenger of Allah! is this 'victory'?" He replied: "By Him in whose Hand is my life, this is indeed 'a manifest Victory'!"

Separately, Ibn Kathir cites Imam Aḥmad's report from ʿUmar about a journey on which he had questioned the Prophet ﷺ three times without receiving an answer, and then heard himself called back. The Prophet ﷺ said to him:

> "Last night, a Surah was revealed to me that is dearer to me than this life and all that it contains."

Ibn Kathir notes that al-Bukhārī, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʼī collected this ḥadīth from several chains of narration through Mālik, and that ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī called it a good chain of narration consisting of the scholars of Madinah.

Ibn Kathir glosses **fatḥan mubīnā** simply as "clear and apparent victory." Ibn Masʿūd and other Companions said, "You consider the conquering of Makkah to be Al-Fath, while to us, Al-Fath is the treaty conducted at Al-Hudaybiyyah." Jābir said, "We only considered Al-Fath to be the day of Hudaybiyyah!" Al-Bukhārī records al-Barāʼ saying, "You consider Al-Fath to be the conquest of Makkah, which was indeed a victory. However, we consider Al-Fath to be the pledge of Ar-Ridwan on the Day of Al-Hudaybiyyah."

The sources spell out why. Because peace made the road safe: people met each other openly, the believers preached to the idolaters, and beneficial knowledge and faith spread all around. Because the misplaced obstinacy of Quraysh became manifest and a schism arose among them — Budayl ibn Warqāʼ separated with his comrades, and ʿUrwah ibn Masʿūd with his group. Because ʿUrwah, sent to negotiate, went back and told the Quraysh leaders, "I have been to the courts of the Caesar and Khosroes, and the Negus also, but never have I seen any people so devoted to a king as are the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ to him." Because Arab delegations came to him, letters were sent to the rulers of the world, Khaybar was conquered in the year 7 after the Hijrah, and where there had been no more than fifteen hundred Muslims with him at Hudaybiyah, afterwards people entered Allah's religion in throngs — so that when Quraysh violated the terms, the Prophet ﷺ within twenty-one months marched towards Makkah with ten thousand, and Quraysh were so overwhelmingly subdued that no fighting took place. The Companions fearlessly performed ṭawāf, and the Prophet ﷺ entered the Kaʿbah, where he received its keys. At that moment he addressed ʿUmar in particular and the Companions in general: "This is the incident that I have been narrating to you." At the Farewell Pilgrimage he repeated the address, and ʿUmar replied: "Undoubtedly there is no better and greater 'Victory' than the Treaty of Hudaibiyah."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion: Abū Bakr believed from the very outset that Hudaybiyah was indeed the victory, but people did not have the insight to discern the reality that had been determined between Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. Allah does not do anything because of people's impatience; He does what His wisdom demands, so that everything takes place at the right moment.

## What the victory was for

Ayah 2 opens with the prefixed **li-** — *li-yaghfira laka'llāh*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that if this particle *lām* is taken to be for *taʿlīl* — stating a cause or a purpose — then it indicates the reason why such a manifest victory was given to the Prophet ﷺ: to bless him with three different bounties.

**The first bounty: forgiveness — "what went before of your sin and what came after."** Ibn Kathir says this clause contains one of the special virtues of the Messenger ﷺ, and that no one else shares this honour with him: there is not an authentic ḥadīth stating that any person other than him earned forgiveness for all his sins of the past and the future on account of performing good deeds. It is the honour of the one who fulfilled the requirements of Allah's obedience, righteousness and straightness at a level never surpassed by a human being in past generations, nor ever to be surpassed in the generations to come.

What, then, does *dhanb* — usually rendered "sin" or "fault" — mean here? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazharī, explains that all the Prophets are infallible, and that where words like *dhanb* and *ʿiṣyān* are attributed to them in the Qurʼan, they are in relation to their lofty status: works that are merely unadvisable, contrary to the preferred practice, are called *dhanb* at that height by way of reprimand. "Previous" refers to shortcomings before the conferment of prophethood, and "subsequent" to those after it. Maʿārif also gives a reason why this victory *caused* that forgiveness: large masses of people entered the fold of Islam after it, the credit for spreading that call goes to the Prophet ﷺ for which he deserved the divine reward, and an increase in reward always entails the forgiveness of shortcomings.

Ibn Kathir cites Imam Aḥmad's report from Anas ibn Mālik that this ayah was revealed on the return from Hudaybiyah, and that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Tonight, an Ayah, that is dearer to me than all that the earth carries, was revealed to me." He recited it to them, and they said, "Congratulations, O Allah's Messenger! Allah has stated what He will do with you. So what will He do with us?" — whereupon the ayat about admitting the believing men and the believing women to Gardens under which rivers flow, ending in *a supreme success*, were revealed. This ḥadīth, Ibn Kathir notes, is recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs.

Ibn Kathir also cites Imam Aḥmad's report from al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah that he used to pray until both his feet were swollen. Asked whether Allah had not already forgiven him all his sins of the past and of the future, he answered:

> "Should I not be a thankful servant?"

Ibn Kathir adds that the two collectors of the Ṣaḥīḥs recorded this ḥadīth, as did the rest of the Group except Abū Dāwūd.

**"And complete His favour on you."** Ibn Kathir's gloss on this clause is brief and comprehensive — "in this life and the Hereafter."

**The second bounty: guidance to a straight path.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises what it calls a question of the highest significance: the Prophet ﷺ was established in the right path from the very outset, and was not only on it himself but a source of guidance for the entire world — so what does guidance to the straight path through a manifest victory in the sixth year of the Hijrah mean? Two answers appear in the sources. Ibn Kathir reads the clause as guidance "with the glorious legislation and the straight religion that He ordains on you" — the path being the revealed law itself. Maʿārif answers from the meaning of *hidāyah*, which it defines as showing the path, or leading someone gently and kindly towards his destination. Man's real destination is to attain Allah's pleasure and His proximity, and the degrees of that pleasure and proximity are unlimited: having attained the first, one needs to go for the next, and so on to no end. No man — no Muslim, no saint, no prophet — is above the need for such spiritual and moral attainment. This is why the prayer for right guidance in the first sūrah is addressed not only to the Muslim community but to the Prophet ﷺ as well; he is to soar higher and higher. In this manifest victory, Maʿārif says, Allah raised him to the highest pinnacles of spiritual eminence.

**The third bounty: mighty support.** *Wa yanṣuraka'llāhu naṣran ʿazīzā.* Ibn Kathir ties it directly to what the Prophet ﷺ had just done: due to your obedience of the orders of Allah, Allah will elevate your status and give you victory above your enemies. Maʿārif observes that he had always had help from Allah, but on this occasion he received a very large share of it.

Ibn Kathir then quotes a ḥadīth he describes as authentic — without naming the collection:

> "No servant pardons but Allah grants him honour, and none humbles himself for Allah except that Allah the exalted and sublime raises him in rank."

ʿUmar, who had struggled hardest with the treaty, put the same principle in a sentence Ibn Kathir preserves: "You will never punish someone who disobeyed Allah with you better than obeying Allah with him."

## What it asks of us

The passage is about how Allah's help actually arrives. It rarely looks like what we asked for.

So: obey first and understand later, as the Prophet ﷺ did when Qaṣwāʼ knelt. Trust that a delayed promise is not a broken one — "did I promise that it will happen this year?" Take ʿUmar's honesty as permission to admit an unsettled heart, and take his response — seeking refuge with Allah from Shayṭān, voluntary prayer, voluntary fasting, freeing slaves, giving alms — as what to do with it, rather than nursing it. Lead by doing, as Umm Salamah advised: shave your own head first. And when Allah forgives, let the Prophet's ﷺ swollen feet set the standard for what gratitude looks like.

Imam Aḥmad recorded from ʿAbdullāh ibn Mughaffal that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited Sūrah al-Fatḥ on the day of the conquest of Makkah, riding on his she-camel, in a vibrating and pleasant tone — the promise recited aloud on the day it came true. Both al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded this ḥadīth, through Shuʿbah.

passages.title: Serenity sent down and the hosts of Allah
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are the answer to a question the Companions actually asked. What holds them together is a single movement: one act of Allah — sending down serenity into the hearts of the believers — followed by a chain of consequences that the passage itself lays out in order: *that they may grow more in faith along with their faith*, *that He may admit* the believing men and women to Gardens, *and that He may punish* the hypocrites and the idolaters. And the whole stretch is framed at both ends by the same sentence: **to Allah belong the armies of the heavens and the earth**. Whatever is said in between about hearts, about Gardens, about Hell, sits inside that frame.

## The question behind the passage

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene plainly. The first three ayat of this surah spoke of Allah's particular bounties bestowed upon the Prophet ﷺ in the wake of the manifest victory. Some of the participants of Hudaybiyyah, congratulating the Prophet ﷺ, asked him that the favours are conferred exclusively upon him — but what is there in it for them? In response to that query, says Maʿārif, ayat 4–7 were revealed. They refer distinctly to the good graces of Allah upon the participants of Hudaybiyyah and of the Pledge of Ridwan, bestowed upon them because of faith in, and obedience to, the Prophet ﷺ. And then the door is opened wide: **all believers whose faith and obedience are complete and perfect will receive similar good graces of Allah.**

Ibn Kathir preserves the same exchange in the narration of Anas, in which the Companions said: "Congratulations, O Allah's Messenger! This good news is for you, so what good news do we have?" — and Allah sent down the words about admitting the believing men and the believing women to Gardens. (Ibn Kathir mentions this from Anas without naming a collection here, so we take the teaching as he gives it, without attaching it to a named book.)

Feel the tenderness of that. They did not complain; they congratulated their Prophet ﷺ first, and only then asked. And the answer that came down was not a rebuke for asking. It was Gardens.

## Serenity, sent down

**هُوَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أَنزَلَ ٱلسَّكِينَةَ فِى قُلُوبِ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ** — *He it is Who sent down As-Sakinah into the hearts of the believers.* Ibn Kathir glosses **sakīnah** in a single word: **tranquility**. Qatadah, the early commentator, calls it "Grace into the hearts of the believers" — meaning, Ibn Kathir explains, the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, on the Day of Al-Hudaybiyyah.

Note where the calm came from and where it landed. The ayah does not say the Companions steadied themselves; it says He sent it down, and it says the place it entered was their hearts. The composure of that day was a gift placed inside the people who were being asked to accept terms that did not look, on the surface, like victory at all.

Ibn Kathir then traces exactly how that stillness came about, and this is the spiritual engine of the entire passage:

> "The companions were they, who accepted the call of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and obeyed the decisions of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. When their hearts felt content with acceptance and were at peace, Allah increased their faith, joining it to the faith they already had."

Read the sequence slowly: **acceptance → contentment of heart → increase of faith.** They submitted to a decision they did not fully understand; their hearts settled; Allah then added to what was already there.

That increase is what the ayah names next: **لِيَزْدَادُوٓاْ إِيمَـٰنًا مَّعَ إِيمَـٰنِهِمْ** — *that they may grow more in faith along with their faith.* Here Ibn Kathir records a point of creed drawn straight from this wording: **Al-Bukhari, and other Imams, relied on this Ayah as proof that faith increases and decreases in the hearts.** The ayah is not describing people acquiring faith for the first time; it describes faith added to faith. On the reading those Imams took from it, **īmān** is not a fixed quantity you either have or lack. It thickens and thins. And if it can be increased, it can also diminish — which is why the believer is never finished with it.

## The armies of the heavens and the earth — and why believers still fight

From the inside of a few hearts the ayah opens out to the whole cosmos: **وَلِلَّهِ جُنُودُ ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ** — *and to Allah belong the armies of the heavens and the earth.*

Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah saying that, had He willed, He would have inflicted defeat on the disbelievers — "and had He willed to send only one angel to them, that angel would have brought destruction to all what they had."

That single sentence resets the frame around Hudaybiyyah. The Muslims at the treaty were in no position to impose terms, and the agreement felt one-sided. But the passage insists that the constraint was never a shortage of power. One angel would have ended the matter. So why the treaty, why the waiting, why any fighting at all?

Ibn Kathir gives the answer: "However, Allah the Exalted willed Jihad and fighting to be established for, and by, the believers for great wisdom, clear reasons and unequivocal evidences that He had in all this." The struggle exists **for** the believers — for what it works in them — and **by** them, as their own act, not as a spectacle performed over their heads.

And it is precisely on the heels of that point that the ayah seals itself: "This is why Allah the Great said next," Ibn Kathir writes, **وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَلِيمًا حَكِيمًا** — *and Allah is Ever All-Knower, All-Wise.* Two names offered to a heart that is thinking, *this outcome does not look right to me*: He knows, and He is Wise.

## What the serenity was for

The next ayah continues the same sentence — *That He may admit the believing men and the believing women to Gardens under which rivers flow to abide therein forever.* The serenity, the increase of faith, the armies of the heavens and the earth: all of it was heading somewhere. Three mercies arrive stacked together.

**Permanence.** On *to abide therein forever*, Ibn Kathir says simply: "meaning they will remain in Paradise forever." Not a reward that runs out — a home.

**Erasure.** On **وَيُكَفِّرَ عَنْهُمْ سَيِّـَٔاتِهِمْ**, *and He may expiate from them their sins*, Ibn Kathir unfolds it warmly: "Allah will not punish them for their errors and mistakes. Rather, He will forgive, absolve and pardon them and cover the errors, grant mercy and appreciate." Notice the ordinary words — **errors and mistakes**. Even the generation praised in this surah had them. The promise is not that they were faultless; it is that Allah covers.

**The verdict.** *And that is with Allah supreme success.* Ibn Kathir defines what "success" means by bringing a parallel ayah: **"And whoever is removed away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise, he indeed is successful"** (Āl ʿImrān 3:185). On Allah's own accounting, success is not a treaty clause going your way. It is clearing the Fire and entering the Garden.

And notice who is named: **the believing men and the believing women.** The question had come from men who stood at Hudaybiyyah; the answer names believing women alongside them — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, reaches every believer whose faith and obedience are complete and perfect.

## The other side of the ledger

The chain of purposes runs on, and turns: **وَيُعَذِّبَ** — *and that He may punish* — the hypocrites, men and women, and the idolaters, men and women.

Their defining trait is named with precision: **ٱلظَّآنِّينَ بِٱللَّهِ ظَنَّ ٱلسَّوْءِ** — *who think evil thoughts about Allah.* Ibn Kathir says exactly what those thoughts were: they are the ones "who question the wisdom in Allah's decisions and think that the Messenger ﷺ and his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, might be killed and exterminated."

This is the hinge of the passage, and it is worth stating starkly. Two groups faced the same ambiguous, unpromising event. Into one group's hearts serenity was sent, and their faith grew. The other group looked at the same event and concluded that Allah's decision was unwise and that His Messenger ﷺ was finished. The difference between the Gardens and the Fire in these ayat is not information — both parties watched the same treaty being signed. It is **what a person assumes about Allah when the outcome is unclear.**

The consequences then arrive in sequence, as Ibn Kathir renders them: *for them is a disgraceful torment. And the anger of Allah is upon them, and He has cursed them* — the curse explained by its effect, "He has cast them away from His mercy" — *and prepared Hell for them, and worst indeed is that destination.*

## The refrain returns

Then the frame closes. The final ayah repeats the sentence from ayah 4 word for word — **وَلِلَّهِ جُنُودُ ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ** — and changes the pair of names at the end: not *All-Knower, All-Wise* this time, but **وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًا**, *All-Powerful, All-Wise.*

Ibn Kathir reads the repetition here as Allah "asserting His ability to take revenge from the enemies of Islam and all disbelievers and hypocrites." The same truth about the armies of the heavens and the earth that reassured the believers at the start of the passage stands over the hypocrites and the idolaters at its end.

## Living it

**Serenity is given, not achieved.** The ayah tells you where calm in a hard moment comes from: Allah sends it down into hearts. So it is something to ask Him for, not something to squeeze out of yourself.

**Obedience comes before the peace, not after it.** In Ibn Kathir's account, the Companions first accepted the call and obeyed the decisions of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ; *then* their hearts were content and at peace; *then* Allah increased their faith. Waiting until you feel settled before you submit reverses the order the passage describes.

**Your faith is a moving quantity.** Al-Bukhari and other Imams took this very ayah as proof that faith increases and decreases in the hearts. That is both a warning and an encouragement — and note the circumstances under which it grew here: a day that looked like a concession.

**Guard your assumptions about Allah.** Thinking badly of Allah — questioning the wisdom in His decisions, expecting His Messenger ﷺ and his people to be finished — is what marks out the people of the Fire in this passage. It is not a private mood; it is the trait the ayah names. When a decree lands that you cannot make sense of, the response the passage hands you is the pair of names it closes with the first time: **All-Knower, All-Wise.**

**And measure success as Allah measures it.** Hudaybiyyah looked like a loss on paper. The passage relocates the whole scoreboard: your errors covered, and a Garden you never leave — *that* is supreme success. Everything short of it is an interim result.

passages.title: The Messenger's mission and the pledge of allegiance
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat move from who the Prophet ﷺ is, to what his mission asks of those who accept him, to the moment in which that acceptance was acted out: believers at Al-Hudaybiyyah placing their hands in his hand, and Allah declaring that those who pledge to His Messenger ﷺ are pledging to Allah Himself.

**What holds them together.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the thread. The verses just before this referred to the favours Allah bestowed generously upon the Prophet ﷺ and his Ummah, especially upon those who took part in the pledge of Ridwan. The Bestower of those favours is Allah, and the medium is the Prophet ﷺ. Therefore, in this set of verses, the right of the Prophet ﷺ and the obligation of the Ummah to honour and revere him is entrenched.

## Ayah 8: three attributes of the Messenger ﷺ

**Witness (shāhid).** Ibn Kathir says he is a witness "of the creation." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties the word to its use in 4:41 — "How would it, then, be when We shall bring a witness from every community and shall bring you over them as a witness." Every prophet will bear testimony that he delivered Allah's message to his particular community — some accepted and others rejected. Likewise the Prophet ﷺ will bear witness for his community.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a genuine difference. Qurṭubī, writing under 4:41, holds that the prophets' testimony will be for the people of their respective time as to who accepted their call to the Truth and who defied it, and likewise the Prophet's ﷺ testimony will be for the people of his particular time. Other scholars express the view that he ﷺ will bear witness to the entire community's good and bad works, and to its obedience and defiance, because, according to some versions, the angels present the works of the community to him morning and evening.

**Bearer of glad tidings (mubashshir).** Ibn Kathir: to the believers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: he gives glad tidings of Paradise to the believing and obedient sector of the community.

**Warner (nadhīr).** Ibn Kathir: to the disbelievers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: he is a warner to those who rejected the message, making them aware of the punishment of such defiance.

## Ayah 9: the purpose — and a famous question about a pronoun

Ibn Kathir renders the ayah keeping the three verbs in Arabic: "In order that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger and that you *Tuʿazziruh* and *Tuwaqqiruh*, and *Tusabbiḥuh Bukrah* and *Aṣīla*."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens each of the three verbs:

- **Tuʿazzirūhu** — from *taʿzīr*, which denotes to help or support. Punishment is also called *taʿzīr*, because the idea underlying punishment is to give real help to the criminal by punishing him (Rāghib, *Mufradāt al-Qurʼān*). Ibn Kathir notes that ʿAbdullah bin ʿAbbas and several others explain the verb as "you honour him."
- **Tuwaqqirūhu** — from *tawqīr*, which means to show reverence. Ibn Kathir glosses *tawqīr* as respect, honour and high regard.
- **Tusabbiḥūhu** — from *tasbīḥ*, which connotes to declare the purity of Allah. Ibn Kathir renders it "glorify Allah's praises," and explains *bukratan wa aṣīlan* as the early and late part of the day.

**Who is "him"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles it carefully. In the third phrase, the attached pronoun refers, by consensus of the grammarians of the Qurʼān, to "Allah", and there can be no other possibility. Therefore most of them believe that the pronouns attached to the verbs of the first two phrases also refer to Allah, giving: believe in Allah and help His religion and His Messenger ﷺ, revere Him, and pronounce His purity. Other scholars refer the pronouns of the first two phrases to the Messenger ﷺ: help the Messenger and revere him, and pronounce the purity of Allah. A third group of scholars feels that this second interpretation involves *intishār al-ḍamāʼir* — an unconcentrated distribution of pronouns, which leads to pronominal ambiguity and is not in conformity with the rules of Arabic rhetoric, *ʿilm al-balāghah*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the discussion with the scholar's formula: *Allah knows best.*

Whichever reading is taken, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out three qualities the believers must be characterized by: that they should "support him"; "and revere him"; and "pronounce His (Allah's) purity morning and evening."

## Ayah 10: the pledge, and the crisis that produced it

Ibn Kathir identifies the pledge in ayah 10 precisely: it is the pledge of **Ar-Ridwan**, pledged under a tree — a *samurah*, described in one narration as a kind of thorny tree — in the area of Al-Hudaybiyyah.

Muhammad bin Isḥāq bin Yasār, in his book on the Sīrah, tells how it came about. The Prophet ﷺ beckoned ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb in order to send him to Makkah, so that he could inform the chiefs of Quraysh of the Prophet's intent to perform ʿUmrah. ʿUmar answered that he feared the Quraysh for himself: no chiefs of his tribe, Banū ʿAdī bin Kaʿb, remained in Makkah who would protect him, and the Quraysh knew his enmity and harshness against them. He proposed a man mightier than himself in Makkah — ʿUthmān bin ʿAffān — to be sent to Abū Sufyān and the chiefs of Quraysh, informing them that the Prophet ﷺ had not come to fight them, but to visit this House and to honour its holiness.

ʿUthmān left for Makkah. On entering, he met Abān bin Saʿīd bin al-ʿĀṣ, who extended his protection to him, so that he could deliver the message. ʿUthmān went to Abū Sufyān and the chiefs of Quraysh and imparted the message he was sent with. When he finished, they said to him: if you wish, you can perform ṭawāf around the House. ʿUthmān replied that he would not do that before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ got the chance to perform ṭawāf around it.

So Quraysh kept ʿUthmān waiting in Makkah. Then the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims were told that ʿUthmān had been killed. Ibn Isḥāq relates, from ʿAbdullah bin Abū Bakr, that when the news of ʿUthmān's death was conveyed to him, the Prophet ﷺ said, "We will not leave until we fight the people." He then called the Muslims to give a pledge of allegiance, and the pledge of Ar-Ridwan was conducted under the tree. Soon afterwards, news came to the Prophet ﷺ that the story of ʿUthmān's death was not true.

Ibn Isḥāq records that the Muslims gave their pledge and none among them held back from giving it, except al-Jadd bin Qays of the tribe of Banū Salamah; Jabir used to say afterwards, "By Allah, it is as if I am looking at him now next to the shoulder of his camel taking refuge behind it, so that the people did not see him."

**How many were they?** Ibn Kathir reports the figures given — 1,300, 1,400 or 1,500 — and says 1,400 is the better choice. Al-Bukhari records Jabir bin ʿAbdullah saying, "We numbered one thousand and four hundred on the day of Hudaybiyyah," and Muslim also collected it; another narration collected in the Two Sahihs from Jabir gives one thousand and five hundred. Al-Bukhari also records that Qatādah asked Saʿīd bin al-Musayyib how many were present for the pledge of Ar-Ridwan; Saʿīd said one thousand and five hundred. Qatādah put to him that Jabir had said one thousand and four hundred, and Saʿīd answered, "He forgot. He told me that they were one thousand and five hundred." Al-Bayhaqī comments that this narration testifies that Jabir used to state they were one thousand and five hundred, but later remembered the true number and said one thousand and four hundred.

**ʿUmar's story.** Al-Bukhari records from Nāfiʿ that on the Day of Hudaybiyyah ʿUmar sent ʿAbdullah to bring a horse he kept with a man from the Anṣār, so that he could use it to fight. The Prophet ﷺ was then taking the pledge from the Muslims under the tree while ʿUmar was unaware. ʿAbdullah conducted his pledge, fetched the horse and brought it to ʿUmar, who was wearing his armour in preparation for battle, and told him that the Messenger of Allah was accepting the pledge under the tree; ʿUmar proceeded with ʿAbdullah and gave his pledge. Nāfiʿ notes that this is why some people thought ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar embraced Islam before ʿUmar, which is not true. In a ḥadīth collected by Muslim, Jabir bin ʿAbdullah says that they gave the pledge while ʿUmar was holding the Prophet's ﷺ hand under the tree.

## What exactly did they pledge?

Here the narrations differ, and both sides are in the strongest collections. Ibn Kathir records both.

Ibn Isḥāq notes that people used to say the Prophet ﷺ took the pledge from them to die; but Jabir bin ʿAbdullah said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not ask us to give a pledge to die (or be victorious), but that we would not run away (from battle)." In a ḥadīth collected by Muslim, Jabir says the same directly: "We gave the pledge to him not to run away (from battle). We did not give the pledge to die." Muslim also records Maʿqil bin Yasār, who was holding a branch of that tree away from the Prophet's ﷺ head while the pledge was taken: "We were fourteen hundred. We did not give him our pledge to die, but gave the pledge not to run from battle."

Al-Bukhari, however, records Salamah bin al-Akwaʿ saying, "I gave the pledge to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ under the tree," and when Yazīd asked him what he pledged to at that time, he answered, "To die!" Al-Bukhari collected a second ḥadīth from Salamah with the same answer, Muslim collected it as well, and al-Bukhari also collected from ʿAbbād bin Tamīm that the pledge they gave was to die.

**Salamah's own account**, recorded by al-Bayhaqī: they numbered fourteen hundred and reached a well whose water was barely sufficient for the fifty or so sheep drinking from it. The Prophet ﷺ sat on its rim, invoked Allah and spat in the well, and its water gushed out; they watered their animals and drank from it themselves. Then he called the people to give the pledge while he was under the tree, and Salamah was among the first. When about half the people had pledged, the Prophet ﷺ said to him, "Give me the pledge, O Salamah!" Salamah said he had already pledged with the first group. "Do it again." He also saw that Salamah was not wearing armour, and gave him some. When the people were about to finish, he asked once more; Salamah protested that he had pledged at the beginning and in the middle; "Do it again" — so he pledged a third time. The Prophet ﷺ then asked where the armour he had given him had gone. Salamah said ʿĀmir had met him without a shield, so he had given it to him. The Prophet ﷺ laughed and said, "You are just like the man of old times who said, 'O Allah! Give me a dear person who is dearer to me than myself!'"

The Two Sahihs record from Jabir that they numbered one thousand and four hundred, and that the Prophet ﷺ placed his hand in the water and it started gushing forth from between his fingers until everyone had quenched their thirst. Another narration mentions that when the Companions became thirsty on the day of Al-Hudaybiyyah he gave them an arrow from his quiver, which they placed in the well of Al-Hudaybiyyah, and the water gushed out until all had satisfied their thirst. Asked how many they were, Jabir said, "We were one thousand and four hundred. And had we been a hundred thousand, that water would still have been sufficient to satisfy us all."

## "The Hand of Allah is over their hands"

Ibn Kathir first notes that Allah honours, regards and praises His Messenger ﷺ by saying, "Verily, those who give pledge to you, they are giving pledge to Allah," and cites 4:80, "He who obeys the Messenger, has indeed obeyed Allah." On the phrase itself he comments: it means He is with them, hearing their statements and witnessing their stand, having full knowledge of them inwardly and outwardly; therefore Allah was indeed taking the pledge from them through His Messenger ﷺ. He then cites 9:111: "Verily, Allah has purchased of the believers their lives and their properties for which theirs shall be the Paradise… And who is truer to his covenant than Allah? Then rejoice in the bargain you have concluded. That is the supreme success."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the creedal note. The purpose of the believers in entering into the pledge at the hands of the Prophet ﷺ was to act upon the command of Allah and to receive His good pleasure; therefore, when the blessed Companions placed their hands on the hand of the Prophet ﷺ, it was tantamount to taking the pledge at the hands of Allah. As for "Allah's hand," it falls in the category of *mutashābihāt* — those texts whose correct nature cannot be known to us, and whose reality we should not attempt to investigate.

## Breaking the pledge, and keeping it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word *bayʿah*: lexically it connotes a pledge to do some particular work. The ancient and traditional method of this pledge is for the pledging parties to place their hands upon each other, although the placing of hands is not a necessary condition. Once the pledge is consummated, it is juristically binding, and its violation is unlawful.

Hence the two halves at the end of ayah 10. Whoever violates the pledge will cause loss to himself — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: it will not cause loss to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. And whoever fulfils the terms of the pledge will receive a mighty reward from Allah — which Ibn Kathir glosses as a generous reward.

## Honours given to the people of the tree

Ibn Kathir gathers what was said about them:

- Al-Ḥumaydī records from ʿAmr, who heard Jabir say that on the day of Hudaybiyyah they were one thousand and four hundred and the Prophet ﷺ said to them, "Today, you are the best people on the earth."
- Imam Ahmad records from Jabir that the Prophet ﷺ said, "None among those who gave the pledge under the tree shall enter Hellfire."
- ʿAbdullah bin Imam Ahmad records from Jabir that the Prophet ﷺ said, "He who ascends Thaniyyah (i.e. a mountainous pass), the Thaniyyah of Al-Murar, will have as much of his sins relieved for him as the sins that were relieved from the Children of Israel." The first to ascend that hill were the horsemen of Banū al-Khazraj, then the Muslims followed. The Prophet ﷺ said, "All of you will be forgiven, except the owner of the red camel" — a man who, when they urged him to come and have the Messenger of Allah ask forgiveness for him, said that finding his lost camel was dearer to him. Muslim collected this ḥadīth from ʿUbaydullah, from Jabir.
- Muslim records that Abū az-Zubayr heard Jabir say that Umm Mubashshir told him she heard the Prophet ﷺ say, while he was with Ḥafṣah, "Allah willing, none of the Companions of the tree, who gave the pledge under it, will ever enter Hellfire." Ḥafṣah cited 19:71, "There is not one of you but will pass over it," and the Prophet ﷺ responded with what Allah said next, 19:72: "Then We shall save those who had Taqwa and We shall leave the wrongdoers therein on their knees."
- Muslim also narrates from Jabir that a slave of Ḥāṭib bin Abī Baltaʿah came complaining against Ḥāṭib and saying he would surely enter Hell; the Prophet ﷺ replied, "You lie, he shall never enter the Fire; he participated in Badr and Al-Hudaybiyyah."

Ibn Kathir says this is why Allah praised these Companions in ayah 10, and cites 48:18: "Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they gave the pledge to you under the tree, He knew what was in their hearts, and He sent down tranquillity upon them, and He rewarded them with a near victory." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the significance of the pledge of Ridwan is described later in the Surah.

**The tree that could not be found.** The Two Sahihs record that Saʿīd bin al-Musayyib's father was among those who gave the pledge under the tree; he said that in the following year they went for Hajj and could not find the tree. Sufyān commented that the Companions later differed over the location of the tree of Al-Hudaybiyyah, and the Two Sahihs collected that statement from him. Jabir said, "If I still had my sight, I would have shown you the tree."

## Living it

Ayah 9 sets out three qualities that must mark the believer: supporting him, revering him, and pronouncing Allah's purity morning and evening. Ayah 10 sets the standard for commitment. Once given, a pledge is binding and breaking it is unlawful. Fourteen hundred gave their hands under that tree, and Allah, as Ibn Kathir observes, praised them for it in this very ayah.

passages.title: The bedouins' excuses for staying behind
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat expose a lie before it is even spoken. Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ, in advance, the excuse that certain desert Arabs will offer for not marching with him — and then, one layer at a time, strips that excuse away until the real reason underneath it is showing. What holds the passage together is a single movement: from the words on their tongues (ayah 11), to the thought in their hearts (ayah 12), to the verdict this earns (ayah 13), and finally to the One in whose hands both forgiveness and punishment actually rest (ayah 14).

## The moment behind the words

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān places this passage: the reference is to those bedouin tribes who were invited by Allah's Messenger ﷺ to join the party of 1,400 Muslims who were marching to Hudaybiyyah, but who, on one pretext or another, requested to be excused.

Ibn Kathir frames the passage under the heading of the fabricated excuse offered by those who lagged behind and did not participate at Hudaybiyyah, together with Allah's warning for them. They were, he says, bedouins who preferred to remain in their homes and possessions and did not join the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

That is the situation these ayat address: an invitation, and a set of men who each found a reason to be let off.

## Ayah 11: an excuse written out before it was said

The ayah opens with **سَيَقُولُ** — "will say." The Prophet ﷺ is being handed their script before they arrive to recite it. Allah informs His Messenger ﷺ, as Ibn Kathir puts it, of the excuses that the bedouins who lagged behind would offer him. They are named **ٱلْمُخَلَّفُونَ** — rendered "those who stayed behind," and by Ibn Kathir "those who lagged behind" — **مِنَ ٱلْأَعْرَابِ**, from among the desert Arabs.

Their line is: **شَغَلَتْنَآ أَمْوَٰلُنَا** — "our possessions occupied us," and with them, their families. Notice how respectable it sounds. Not "we were afraid," not "we thought you would lose." Rather: we were *busy*. Property to look after, dependants to protect. Ibn Kathir's paraphrase keeps the flavour of the thing: they offered an excuse for lagging behind, as that of being busy — in their homes and with their wealth.

Then comes the request that gives them away: **"so ask forgiveness for us."** On the surface this is a beautiful thing to ask of a prophet. But Ibn Kathir says plainly why they asked: they asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to invoke Allah to forgive them, not because they had faith in the Prophet ﷺ and his invocation, but to show off and pretend. The request for forgiveness was a piece of theatre — a way of buying back their standing without ever admitting what they had actually done.

And so Allah says of them: **يَقُولُونَ بِأَلْسِنَتِهِم مَّا لَيْسَ فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ** — "they say with their tongues what is not in their hearts." That single clause is the hinge of the whole passage. The rest of these ayat is simply Allah opening the gap between the tongue and the heart wide enough for everyone to see through it.

## "Who has any power for you against Allah?"

The Prophet ﷺ is told to answer them with a question rather than an argument: **قُلْ فَمَن يَمْلِكُ لَكُم مِّنَ اللَّهِ شَيْئًا إِنْ أَرَادَ بِكُمْ ضَرًّا أَوْ أَرَادَ بِكُمْ نَفْعًا** — "Say: who then has any power at all, to intervene on your behalf with Allah, if He intends you hurt or intends you benefit?"

Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and complete: none can resist what Allah has decided in your case; all praise and honour belong to Him.

This answer lands exactly on the wound. These men stayed home to keep harm away from their wealth and families and to protect their own benefit. Allah's reply takes both of the words they were quietly relying on — *hurt* and *benefit* — and shows them that neither one was ever in their hands. They had rearranged their loyalties to secure an outcome that was never theirs to secure. Staying behind bought them nothing.

And the section closes with a divine name that answers the tongue-versus-heart problem directly: **بَلْ كَانَ اللَّهُ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ خَبِيرًا** — "Nay, but Allah is Ever All-Aware of what you do." Ibn Kathir: Allah is the Knower of your secrets and what your hearts conceal, even if you pretend and choose to be hypocritical with us. The practical force of it here is stark: an excuse can satisfy a community, and even pass outwardly before a prophet, and still be perfectly transparent to Allah.

## Ayah 12: the reason they did not say out loud

**بَلْ ظَنَنتُمْ أَن لَّن يَنقَلِبَ الرَّسُولُ وَالْمُؤْمِنُونَ إِلَىٰ أَهْلِيهِمْ أَبَدًا** — "Nay, but you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families."

That second **بَلْ** ("nay, but") is the ayah pulling the mask off. The first *bal* corrected their words; this one names their motive. Ibn Kathir voices it in the second person, as the ayah does: *your lagging behind was not an excusable act or just a sin. Rather, your lagging behind was because of hypocrisy and because you thought that the Muslims would be killed to the extent of extermination, their lives would be extinguished and none of them will ever come back.*

Read the two ayat side by side and the deceit is complete. Their excuse leaned on their own households — possessions and families that needed them at home. What they had actually concluded was that the Messenger ﷺ and the believers would never see their families again. They kept their own, and had privately written off the others.

Then: **"and that was made fair seeming in your hearts."** This is how a cowardly calculation survives inside a person: it does not feel like betrayal, it feels like prudence. It is dressed up until it looks like the sensible thing.

**وَظَنَنتُمْ ظَنَّ السَّوْءِ** — "and you did think an evil thought." Allah's verdict on their reading of the situation is not that it was a miscalculation but that it was *evil*. And Ibn Kathir has already told us what lay beneath it: hypocrisy.

## The word that ends the ayah: **بُور**

**وَكُنتُمْ قَوْمًا بُورًا** — "and you became a people *būr*." Ibn Kathir gives us the range of the early explanations rather than one flat translation:

- **Going for destruction** — according to ʿAbdullah bin ʿAbbas, Mujahid and several others.
- **Corrupt** — Qatadah's explanation.
- And some said that it is a word used in the Arabic dialect of the area of Oman.

Notice how the ayah does not say they *did* something *būr*; it says they *became a people* *būr*. It is a description of what they had turned into. Their staying behind was not an isolated lapse but the visible symptom of a ruined condition. And in the explanation reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid there is a bitter irony worth sitting with: they stayed home to avoid destruction, and the ayah tells them that destruction is precisely the direction they were already walking in.

## Ayah 13: why the warning names disbelief

**وَمَن لَّمْ يُؤْمِنۢ بِٱللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦ فَإِنَّآ أَعْتَدْنَا لِلْكَٰفِرِينَ** — "And whosoever does not believe in Allah and His Messenger, then verily, We have prepared for the disbelievers a blazing Fire."

Ibn Kathir draws the principle out of it: whoever does not purify his actions outwardly and inwardly for Allah's sake, then Allah the Exalted will punish him in the Blazing Fire, even if he pretends to show people that he follows the faith, contradicting his true creed.

That is the condition being addressed here, and it is worth stating in Ibn Kathir's own terms: a display of faith before people that the person's real creed contradicts. The excuse of ayah 11 was one symptom of it; the thought of ayah 12 was the disease.

Note also the wording of **أَعْتَدْنَا** — "We have prepared." The Fire is not something to be arranged later in response to them. It is already made ready.

## Ayah 14: the passage turns

After all that, this is not where the passage stops — and the placement of ayah 14 is deliberate.

**وَلِلَّهِ مُلْكُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ** — "And to Allah belongs the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth." Ibn Kathir: Allah states that He is the Only Authority, King and Owner Who has full control over the residents of the heavens and earth. This closes the circle opened in ayah 11. They wanted a word from the Prophet ﷺ to cover them, and were asked who could possibly hold any power for them with Allah. Here is the answer laid out plainly: the kingdom is His, entirely.

**يَغْفِرُ لِمَن يَشَاءُ وَيُعَذِّبُ مَن يَشَاءُ** — "He forgives whom He wills, and punishes whom He wills." Both halves belong to Him and neither is forced upon Him by anyone. Forgiveness is not a right that can be claimed off Him by a performance of piety, and punishment is not something He can be prevented from carrying out.

And then, after the Fire of ayah 13, the passage ends on: **وَكَانَ اللَّهُ غَفُورًا رَّحِيمًا** — "And Allah is Forgiving, Most Merciful." Ibn Kathir attaches the description that makes this real rather than sentimental: forgiving and merciful **with those who repent, return and submit to Him with humiliation**.

So the door is not shut. The men described in these ayat are told exactly what they are — and in the same breath told that the One who owns everything forgives whom He wills. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān records that, according to some versions, some of those people later repented and became sincere Muslims. The passage that names them *būr* was not their final sentence.

## What this asks of us

**Watch the gap between the tongue and the heart.** The one clause "they say with their tongues what is not in their hearts" is the whole diagnosis. The remedy is not better speech; it is bringing the heart up to meet what the mouth is already claiming.

**Be suspicious of an excuse that is too respectable.** "My property" and "my family" were the excuse in ayah 11, and they are among the most reusable excuses in existence — precisely because they are genuine responsibilities and because no one can easily challenge them. The test is not whether the excuse sounds good but whether it is the true reason.

**Notice what "being made fair seeming" does.** A person rarely chooses to abandon a duty while calling it abandonment. It gets dressed up first as prudence, realism, or looking after one's own. If a decision to withdraw feels unusually comfortable, that comfort deserves examining.

**Do not calculate Allah out of the outcome.** These men concluded that the Muslims would be wiped out and none of them would ever come back — and Allah calls that conclusion an evil thought, and Ibn Kathir calls what lay under it hypocrisy. The question the Prophet ﷺ was told to put to them stands over every such calculation: who holds any power for you with Allah, if He intends you hurt or benefit?

**Purify the inside as well as the outside.** Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 13 is that the danger is a life arranged to look right before people while the real creed says something else. What is on display is not what is being judged.

**And do not despair of anyone, including yourself.** The passage that exposes them ends with Allah's forgiveness and mercy — with those who repent, return and submit to Him — and some of those very people, we are told, later repented and became sincere Muslims.

passages.title: Claiming the spoils, refusing the fight
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat deal with the men who had excused themselves from the journey to Hudaybiyyah and then, when a rich and winnable campaign appeared on the horizon, asked to come along. Allah exposes the calculation behind their request, closes that particular door to them, and then — in the same breath — opens a different one. What holds ayat 15–17 together is a single moral movement: **the spoils are refused, but the road back is not closed.**

## The moment behind the words

When the Prophet ﷺ set out for ʿUmrah, certain bedouin tribes contrived to remain behind. Ibn Kathir describes them as the bedouins who lagged behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ during the ʿUmrah of Hudaybiyyah.

In the seventh year of the Hijrah, after the Prophet ﷺ had returned from Hudaybiyyah, he intended to march on Khaybar — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records, he took with him only those sincere Muslims who had been with him at Hudaybiyyah and had taken part in the Pledge of Riḍwān.

Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān both describe what happened next: the very bedouins who had stayed home now came forward asking to join the army. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān allows two possible motives, and it is worth holding both. Some guessed Khaybar would be conquered and that they would receive a good share of the booty. Others had perceived the divine blessings Allah bestowed on the Muslims through the expedition of Hudaybiyyah, felt remorse over their wrong decision, and genuinely intended to join this time.

Allah's answer comes in ayah 15: **"Say: 'You shall not follow us; thus Allah has said beforehand.'"** The Prophet ﷺ was ordered to refuse. Ibn Kathir puts the logic in one line — the refusal was *"a punishment that is similar to their error."* They had absented themselves when it was time to fight the enemy and endure with patience; they are now absented from the profit. The penalty is cut to the shape of the offence.

There is a further point in Ibn Kathir worth noticing. Allah had already promised those who were present at Hudaybiyyah that they would earn Khaybar's war spoils **alone**, not shared with the bedouins who lagged behind. So the ruling given here is not an arbitrary rebuke; it is the legal expression of something already decreed. As Ibn Kathir puts it, the legislation Allah gave in this matter "was joined to the destiny that He decided, occurring just as He decided."

## "They want to change the Words of Allah"

The Qur'an characterises their request with startling severity: **يُرِيدُونَ أَن يُبَدِّلُوا كَلَامَ اللَّهِ** — *they want to change Allah's Words.* They thought they were asking a favour of an army commander. They were in fact asking that a divine promise be rewritten.

What are these "Words of Allah"? Ibn Kathir reports the explanation of **Mujāhid, Qatādah and Juwaybir**, which **Ibn Jarīr** preferred: it is the promise Allah gave to those who were present at Hudaybiyyah. And ayah 15 says it plainly — *"thus Allah has said beforehand"* — meaning, as Ibn Kathir glosses it, when He promised the participants of Hudaybiyyah, before you ever asked to join them.

### A door into a much larger question

Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stops and takes up a problem that turns this ayah into one of the strongest Qur'anic proofs for the authority of hadith.

The ruling reserving the right to join the Khaybar expedition and share in its spoils to the participants of Hudaybiyyah **is nowhere stated in the Qur'an.** Yet ayah 15 calls it *"the statement of Allah"* and says *"Allah had said like this beforehand."* How?

The answer, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, lies in the two kinds of revelation:

- **Waḥy Matluww** — "recited revelation": the Qur'an, whose wording *and* meaning are both from Allah.
- **Waḥy Ghayr-Matluww** — "unrecited revelation": the Hadith of the Prophet ﷺ, whose wording is his ﷺ but whose meaning is from Allah.

Unrecited revelation, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states, is — like recited revelation — one of the fundamental sources of Islamic injunctions. The restriction on Khaybar's spoils was conveyed to the Prophet ﷺ as unrecited revelation on his way to Hudaybiyyah — and the Qur'an then refers to that very ruling by the phrases *Kalām Allāh* (the statement of Allah) and *qāla Allāh* (Allah said). From this a general juristic rule is deduced: **injunctions entrenched in *aḥādīth ṣaḥīḥah* — authentic Prophetic traditions — have the status of "Allah's statement" and "Allah's saying."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds that these verses are sufficient to unmask the deviation of those who turn aside from the truth by refusing to accept hadith as a religious authority.

Two counter-proposals are examined and set aside:

**First**, that "the statement of Allah" refers to ayat 18–19 of this same surah — *"so He sent down tranquility upon them, and rewarded them with a well-nigh victory, and many spoils that they would receive"* — revealed at the beginning of the journey to Hudaybiyyah, the "well-nigh victory" being Khaybar according to the consensus of Qur'anic scholars. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that this argument is misconceived: those ayat promise the Hudaybiyyah participants many spoils, but **nowhere say the spoils are restricted to them and that no one else will participate in them.** The restriction — precisely the point at issue — is not in the recited text.

**Second**, that it refers to Sūrah at-Tawbah 83, the ayah in which those who seek permission to march out are told they will never march out with him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān rejects this on plain chronology, citing **Qurṭubī** and others: those ayat pertain to the battle of Tabūk, which took place in the ninth year of the Hijrah, whereas the expedition of Khaybar took place two years earlier, in the seventh. A later revelation cannot be what "Allah said beforehand."

## "Nay, you envy us"

Ayah 15 predicts their reply before they give it: **"Then they will say: 'Nay, you envy us.'"** Ibn Kathir unpacks the accusation — *you do not want us to share the war spoils with you.*

The Qur'an's verdict on that reply is quiet and devastating — **"Nay, but they understand not except a little."** Ibn Kathir: the truth is nothing close to what they claimed, but they understand not.

Notice what this exposes. When a decree of Allah crosses what we want, the cheapest explanation within reach is a low motive in whoever delivers it. And the Qur'an's answer is not an argument but a flat correction: the truth was nothing close to what they claimed. Their confidence in reading the Companions' hearts was, by Allah's own testimony, a failure of understanding.

## The refusal was for Khaybar only

It would be easy to read ayah 15 as a permanent expulsion. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to say it is not. The laggards are emphatically told they could not march against the Jews of Khaybar and partake of the booty — but this prohibition is **restricted to the expedition of Khaybar**; in the near future they would be allowed to fight other battles. The proof is historical: from among these very laggards, the tribes of **Muzaynah and Juhaynah** later fought in the company of the Prophet ﷺ (al-Rūḥ citing al-Baḥr; Bayān).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a fairness that is easy to miss. All the laggards who did not march towards Hudaybiyyah were barred from Khaybar — but **not all of them were hypocrites; some were sincere Muslims.** And some who were hypocrites at that particular time later became sincere Muslims through the Grace of Allah. The bar was a consequence of a promise made to others, not a final judgement on every man's soul.

## Ayah 16: a second summons

This is why ayah 16 reads not as a further scolding but, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, as consolation and comfort: because of Allah's promise to the participants of Hudaybiyyah they cannot join Khaybar — yet in the near future the sincere Muslims would be called upon to fight against much more powerful enemies. **"You will be called against a people possessed of strong fighting power; you will have to fight them, or they will submit."**

You have lost Khaybar. You have not lost your future. Something harder is coming, and you will be invited to it.

**Who are "a people given to great warfare"?** Ibn Kathir records an unusually wide spread of opinion among the early scholars, and it is worth seeing the range rather than a single tidy answer:

- **Hawāzin** — as Shuʿbah narrated from Abū Bishr from Saʿīd bin Jubayr, or ʿIkrimah, or both; Hushaym narrated it from Abū Bishr from both of them; and Qatādah in one narration held the same view.
- **Thaqīf** — Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk.
- **Banū Ḥanīfah** — Juwaybir and az-Zuhrī (as Muḥammad bin Isḥāq narrated from him); similar was narrated from Saʿīd bin Jubayr and ʿIkrimah.
- **The Persians** — ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reporting from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAbbās; also the view of ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah.
- **The Romans** — Kaʿb al-Aḥbār.
- **The Persians and Romans together** — Ibn Abī Laylā, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, and Qatādah in a different narration from him.
- **The idolaters** — Mujāhid.
- **No particular people at all** — Mujāhid in another narration: simply "men given to great warfare." This is the view **Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Jarīr preferred.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues for a deferred fulfilment on historical grounds. The prophecy was not fulfilled in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime. Battles did take place after Khaybar, but there is no proof that the Prophet ﷺ called upon the bedouins to fight; and no battle occurred against a nation whose fighters were as brave, chivalrous and formidable as the ayah describes. At Tabūk the encounter was with a formidable force, but there is no evidence the bedouins were invited, and no actual fighting took place, because Allah had infused terror into the minds of the opponents and they did not turn up. As for Ḥunayn, there is no proof of their being invited, nor was the opponent so powerful.

Hence some of the leading scholars of tafsīr — **Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, Ibn Abī Laylā and al-Ḥasan, as cited by Qurṭubī** — held that the ayah refers to the fierce and protracted wars with the **Byzantine and Iranian empires**, which took place during the reign of Sayyidnā al-Fārūq al-Aʿẓam (may Allah be pleased with him).

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān preserves a beautiful eyewitness note from **Sayyidnā Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj** (may Allah be pleased with him): they used to read this ayah with its word *qawm* — "a people" — and did not know which people were meant, until after the Prophet ﷺ, when Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) took over the reign of the Caliphate and invited them to take up arms against Banū Ḥanīfah, the people of Yamāmah — that is, Musaylimah the Liar. "So we thought the Qur'an refers to this *qawm*."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sees no conflict or contradiction between these views: the word *qawm* is broad enough to comprehend all these nations. And having cited them all, **Imām Qurṭubī** asserts that this ayah confirms the legitimacy of the Caliphate of Sayyidnā Abū Bakr and Sayyidnā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them), since the Qur'an itself speaks of their calling upon the people to fight.

### "…or they shall surrender"

**تُقَاتِلُونَهُمْ أَوْ يُسْلِمُونَ.** Ibn Kathir explains the two outcomes: you are called to fight them in jihād, through constant warfare, until you become victorious over them or they surrender — *or* they will embrace your religion without a fight, but with their full consent.

There is a fine linguistic observation in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān here. In the reading (*qirāʾah*) of Sayyidnā Ubayy, the second clause is *aw yuslimū*, with the final *nūn* omitted. On that basis **Imām Qurṭubī** takes the particle *aw* — ordinarily "or" — in the sense of *ḥattā*, "until." The sense then becomes: the fighting will carry on with that nation **until** they surrender, whether by embracing Islam or by submitting to Islamic rule. A small grammatical shift, and the clause turns from a menu of outcomes into a horizon.

### Obey, and you are not held to your past

The rest of ayah 16 is the offer stated in the plainest terms. Ibn Kathir glosses **"Then if you obey"** as: if you accept the call to jihād, prepare for it, and fulfil your duty in this regard — *"Allah will give you a fair reward."* And the warning: **"but if you turn away as you turned away before"** — Ibn Kathir specifies the reference, *on the day of al-Ḥudaybiyyah, when you were called to jihād, yet lagged behind* — *"He will punish you with a painful torment."*

The past failure is named, but it is named as a pattern to break, not a sentence already passed.

## Ayah 17: the mercy clause

**"There is no blame on the blind, nor is there any blame on the lame, nor is there any blame on the sick."**

There is a moving occasion of revelation for this recorded by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from **Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās** (may Allah be pleased with him), citing Qurṭubī. When some sincere Muslims who were **physically unable to fight** read the concluding clause of ayah 16 — *"And if you turn away, as you had turned away before, He will punish you with a painful punishment"* — they expressed their concern about the warning. Ayah 17 was revealed to exempt them from the injunction of jihād. These people included those who were blind, lame, or sick.

Think about what that tells us. These men were not scheming for spoils; they were afraid of Allah's displeasure over something they physically could not do. And Allah answered their anxiety directly, in revelation, naming their very condition.

Ibn Kathir lists these as the legal reasons that excuse one from joining the jihād: blindness, lameness, and various illnesses that strike a person and are remedied in a few days. His note on the last category matters: when someone is ill he is allowed to remain behind and has a valid excuse **until his illness ends**. A temporary excuse is temporary; it lifts when the cause lifts.

## The two ends of the road

Ayah 17 closes the passage by lifting it out of Khaybar and out of the seventh year of the Hijrah entirely, into a rule that holds for anyone:

**"And whosoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him to Gardens beneath which rivers flow; and whosoever turns back, He will punish him with a painful torment."**

Ibn Kathir glosses *"whosoever turns back"* as the one who turns from joining the jihād and busies himself in his livelihood. And he notes that the painful torment is of two kinds: **in this life, humiliation; in the Hereafter, the Fire.** Then, as is his habit at the edge of what can be known, he closes: *Allah the Exalted has the best knowledge.*

## What this passage asks of us

- **A promise of Allah is not negotiable.** The laggards' request looked reasonable — more men, more strength. But it collided with a divine word, and reasonableness does not outrank revelation.
- **The Sunnah is revelation too.** The clearest lesson of ayah 15, on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, is that Allah Himself calls a ruling delivered through His Messenger ﷺ "the statement of Allah."
- **Absence has a cost, and the cost is precisely shaped.** They withheld themselves from hardship; they were withheld from the reward — a punishment, in Ibn Kathir's words, similar to their error.
- **Be slow to assign low motives.** "Nay, you envy us" was answered by Allah with a flat correction: the truth was nothing close to what they claimed.
- **A closed door is not a closed future.** Muzaynah and Juhaynah, from among these very laggards, later fought alongside the Prophet ﷺ — and ayah 16 held out a summons still to come.
- **Genuine inability is excused.** Ayah 17 exists because sincere believers who could not fight were worried by a warning — and their worry was answered with an exemption, not a rebuke.

passages.title: The pledge beneath the tree and the spoils promised
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat look back at one specific moment — a body of believers gathered under a tree in the area of Hudaybiyyah, placing their hands in the hand of the Prophet ﷺ and pledging themselves to him — and then look forward from that moment across the future of the Muslim community. What holds them together is a single movement: **Allah declares that He was pleased with those who pledged (ayah 18), and then unfolds what that pleasure produced** — His knowledge of their hearts, calm sent down upon them, a victory close at hand, abundant spoils, and beyond them victories still out of reach that Allah has already encircled (ayat 19–21).

## The pledge itself

The pledge referred to here is the same one mentioned earlier in the surah at ayah 10. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that ayah 18 reinforces ayah 10: there Allah described the pledge, and here He announces its outcome — that the sincere participants who took this solemn oath obtained His pleasure. This is exactly why it came to be called **baiʿat-ur-Riḍwān**, "the pledge that earned Allah's pleasure." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the Arabic of ayah 18 with the physical detail intact: they were "pledging allegiance with you by placing their hands in your hands under the tree." That is what a *bayʿah* is — not a mood or a private intention, but hand in hand, a transaction witnessed and binding.

Ibn Kathir records that the number who gave this pledge was **one thousand four hundred**, and that the tree was a *samurah* tree, located in the area of Hudaybiyyah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies it as the gum-acacia (mimosa arabica) and records that it is in Bukhari and Muslim, on the authority of Sayyidnā Jābir (may Allah be pleased with him), that on the day of Hudaybiyah the Companions were 1400 in number, and the Prophet ﷺ said to them: **"You are the best of people living on the surface of the earth."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records that it is in Muslim, on the authority of Umm Bishr (may Allah be pleased with her), that the Prophet ﷺ said: **"None of those who swore fealty under the tree will enter the Fire"** (quoted there from Tafsīr Mazharī).

Notice the purpose Maʿārif ul Qurʼān assigns to the whole announcement: it is **both a compliment and a charge** — to compliment the participants of the allegiance, and to emphasise the obligation of fulfilling the covenant.

## "Allah was pleased" — and what that guarantees

Ayah 18 opens with *la-qad raḍiya llāhu* — rendered "Indeed, Allah was pleased," a statement made with emphasis. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the consequence out plainly: the participants of this allegiance are like the participants of the battle of Badr, for whom the Qur'an and Hadith give glad tidings of Allah's pleasure and Paradise; the sources give the same tidings to the participants of baiʿat-ur-Riḍwān. And these tidings bear testimony to something that had not yet happened when they were given — that these sincere participants would **meet their end in the state of faith, in righteousness, and with deeds that please Allah** — because this announcement of Allah's pleasure guarantees that.

From this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Tafsīr Mazharī) derives a rule of conduct toward the Companions: they are among the best of the Prophet's ﷺ followers, and Allah has announced forgiveness of their sins, shortcomings and slips, if they committed any. It is therefore **against the declaration of this verse to investigate into those of their deeds that are not laudable and to make it a subject of debate**. The same source records that this is a crystal clear denunciation of the attitude of the Rawāfiḍ, who reject the legitimacy of the caliphs Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿUthmān (may Allah be pleased with them) and vilify them and other blessed Companions, condemning them as unbelievers and hypocrites.

## "He knew what was in their hearts"

The pledge was an outward act; ayah 18 immediately moves inward. **Ibn Kathir glosses *fa-ʿalima mā fī qulūbihim* — "He knew what was in their hearts" — as meaning what was there of truthfulness, trustworthiness, obedience and adherence.** The praise is not for the raised hands but for what stood behind them, and only Allah could certify that.

Then: *fa-anzala l-sakīnata ʿalayhim* — "and He sent down as-Sakīnah upon them." **Ibn Kathir explains Sakīnah here as calmness and tranquillity.** Notice the direction of the verb: it was *sent down*. The steadiness in those hearts was not something the men manufactured for themselves; it descended on them as a gift. And notice the order the ayah keeps: Allah's pleasure, then His knowledge of what was in their hearts, then the calm He sent down upon them, then the reward of a near victory. Each link follows from the one before it.

## The tree that was cut down

One of the most striking things in the sources for this passage is not a battle but a felled tree.

Ibn Kathir narrates that **Al-Bukhari** narrated from Ṭāriq that ʿAbdur-Raḥmān said: "I went on Hajj and passed by people praying and asked, 'What is this Masjid?' They said, 'This is the tree where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took the pledge of Ar-Riḍwān.' So I went to Saʿīd bin Al-Musayyib and told him. Saʿīd said, 'My father told me that he was among those who gave their pledge to the Messenger of Allah under the tree. My father said: The following year, when we went out, we forgot its place and could not agree which tree it was.' Saʿīd said, **'The Companions of Muhammad ﷺ forgot where the tree was, but you know where it is. Therefore, you have better knowledge than them!'**"

The sarcasm is the point. The very men whose hands had touched the Prophet's ﷺ hand at that spot could not, a year later, agree on which tree it had been.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the sequel. It is reported that after the Prophet ﷺ, some people used to walk to the site and perform ṣalāh there. Sayyidnā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) came to know of it and feared that a future generation lacking in knowledge might start **worshipping the very tree, as had happened in past generations**. So he had the tree felled. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reasons from the report above that people must have determined conjecturally — on incomplete and doubtful evidence — that a particular tree was the tree of the pledge, and so frequented the place and prayed there; ʿUmar knew it was not the real tree, and he apprehended people's involvement in shirk, so he had it cut down.

This is a rare and instructive thing: a place Allah Himself honours in the Qur'an, and the closest generation of Muslims deliberately declining to turn it into a shrine. **The honour named in ayah 18 belongs to the pledge and to the hearts that gave it — not to the wood.**

## "A near victory" — Khaybar

Ayah 18 ends: *wa-athābahum fatḥan qarīban*, "and He rewarded them with a near victory." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that there is **consensus of the scholars that the "well-nigh victory" here means the victory of Khaybar**, which occurred after the return from Hudaybiyah. Khaybar, it explains (from Mazharī), is the name of a province comprising many settlements, fortresses and gardens — not a single fort.

The timing is close indeed. According to some versions the Prophet ﷺ stayed in Madinah only ten days after returning from Hudaybiyah, and according to others twenty, before marching against Khaybar. In Ibn Isḥāq's version he returned to Madinah in Dhū al-Ḥijjah and set out for Khaybar in Muḥarram of the 7th year of Hijrah. Khaybar was conquered in Ṣafar of that year, as reported in Wāqidī's *Maghāzī*; according to Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar this is the preferred opinion (Tafsīr Mazharī).

That raises a fine point Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles honestly.
