By consensus of scholarly opinion, Sūrah al-Fatḥ was revealed in the course of the return journey from Hudaybiyah — but there is a difference of opinion over whether the surah was revealed in its entirety then or some of its verses were revealed later. **If the first view is preferred, then the conquest of Khaybar is a prophecy stated in the past-perfect tense** — a future event described as though already accomplished, to denote that it is as certain as something that has already happened. If the second view is preferred, it is possible that these verses were revealed after Khaybar was conquered. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān leaves it there: *Allah knows best.*

## The spoils: taken, hastened, and still to come

Ayah 19 — "and many spoils of war they will gain" — refers, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, to the great booty that fell into the hands of the Muslims during the conquest of Khaybar. Ibn Kathir reads ayat 18–19 together as one arc of consequence: on account of the peace treaty between the Companions and their disbelieving enemies, ever after that they **gained abundant, general and continuous benefits and accomplishments, leading to the conquest of Khaybar and Makkah and then the various surrounding provinces and areas** — tremendous glory, triumphs, and an elevated and honourable status in this life and in the Hereafter.

Ayah 19 closes with two names: **ʿAzīz** (All-Mighty) and **Ḥakīm** (All-Wise). Both are needed to read this episode rightly. The might is what turns a treaty into an opening; the wisdom is why the opening came in that form and not another. As Ibn Kathir will say a verse later, the best decisions are the ones Allah prefers for His believing servants, even when those decisions look unfavourable outwardly.

**Ayah 20** then addresses the believers directly: "Allah has promised you abundant spoils, which you will take, and He has hastened this one for you." The commentators read the two halves differently:

- **Mujahid**: the promise refers to the spoils the Muslims earned up until that time; "He has hastened for you this" means the conquest of Khaybar.
- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (reported by Al-ʿAwfī): "He has hastened for you this" means the **peace treaty of Al-Hudaybiyyah** itself.

Read Ibn ʿAbbās's way, the ayah is startling: the "hastened" gift is not gold or land at all, but a treaty.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a detail worth pausing on. It reads the "many spoils" as the sizeable spoils that fell to the Muslims in the conquests which followed the victory at Khaybar, in the rest of Arabia and the neighbouring countries — a prophecy of great victories, and spoils in consequence, until the end of the world. But before those numerous conquests, the conquest of Khaybar was given first, and its spoils were **reserved by Allah exclusively for the participants of Hudaybiyah**, while the spoils of all the later conquests would be common to all. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes candidly that this restriction is not laid down explicitly in these verses; it was laid down in a separate category of revelation — the unrecited revelation, guidance given to the Prophet ﷺ outside the wording of the Qur'an — upon which he ﷺ acted and whose knowledge he imparted to the noble Companions. The reward, in other words, was tied to the men who had stood under the tree.

## "He restrained the hands of men from you"

Ayah 20 credits the safety itself to Allah. Ibn Kathir explains *wa-kaffa aydiya n-nāsi ʿankum* as meaning that no harm the enemies had planned — fighting and warfare — touched them; and further, that Allah **also restrained the hands of the men whom they had left behind, close to their families and children, from harming them**. Protection reached both the men on the road and the households left behind.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies the phrase to the unbelievers of Khaybar, whom Allah did not allow the opportunity to show much strength or force, and quotes Imām Baghawī on a concrete case: the tribe of Ghaṭafān were allies of the Jews of Khaybar, and when they heard of the Prophet's ﷺ march they equipped themselves with heavy arms to defend them — but **Allah infused terror into their minds**, and they were worried that if they went forward a Muslim army might attack their homes in their absence. They got cold feet and did not have the courage to proceed. No sword was needed; a thought was enough.

**"That it may be a sign for the believers"** — Ibn Kathir: a sign with which they take heed and understand, namely that Allah will help and protect the believers against all enemies **even though the believers are few in number**; and that by this the believers will come to know that Allah is truly the Knower of the consequences of all matters, and that the best decisions are the ones He prefers for His believing servants **even though these decisions might look unfavourable outwardly**. He cites the Qur'an's own principle: *"It may be that you dislike a thing that is good for you"* (2:216). That is the interpretive key to the whole episode.

**"And that He may guide you to a straight path"** — Ibn Kathir ties this to their obeying His commands and adhering to His orders by following the path of His Messenger ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens it: there are several degrees of guidance, and from that point of view the Companions were already guided on the straight path. What is meant here is **a degree they had not yet attained — full reliance on Allah and an increase in the power of faith.** Guidance is not only the doorway; it is the whole staircase, and a believer can be genuinely guided and still be given more.

## Ayah 21: victories Allah has already encircled

"And other gains which are beyond your reach that Allah has already encompassed." Ibn Kathir: there are other war spoils and victories to come which are not within your grasp now, **but Allah will make them within your reach, and indeed He encompasses all these victories for your benefit** — and Allah provides provisions and sustenance for His servants who have taqwā (mindfulness of Allah) from resources they could never imagine.

The scholars of tafsir differ over which victories are meant, and Ibn Kathir reports the difference rather than settling it:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (via Al-ʿAwfī): the conquest of **Khaybar** — a meaning Ibn Kathir calls sound, since on that reading "He has hastened for you this" refers to the treaty of Al-Hudaybiyyah. This is also the view of **Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Muhammad bin Isḥāq, and ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam**.
- **Qatādah**: the conquest of **Makkah** — the opinion preferred by **Ibn Jarīr**.
- **Ibn Abī Laylā and Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī**: the victories over the **Persians and the Romans**.
- **Mujahid**: **every** victory and all spoils of war, **until the Day of Resurrection**.

And Abū Dāwūd Aṭ-Ṭayālisī recorded Ibn ʿAbbās commenting on this very phrase: **"They are the victories that are continuing until this day."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reaches a similar conclusion by way of the language: among these victories Makkah was the first to be achieved, which is why some scholars refer the verse there, **but the wordings are general and refer to all the victories that will be achieved till the end of the world** (Mazharī).

The verb *aḥāṭa* — He has encompassed, encircled — is doing the work here. The believers are told plainly that these things are not yet within their power (*lam taqdirū ʿalayhā*); in the same breath they are told the things are already inside Allah's encompassing. Ayah 21 then seals it with **Qadīr**: Allah is Ever Able to do all things. Human incapacity and divine capability are set side by side in one sentence.

## What the passage asks of us

**Take the long view of an outcome you did not choose.** Ibn Kathir reads ayah 20 as teaching precisely this: Allah is the Knower of the consequences of all matters, and the best decisions are the ones He prefers for His servants, even when they look unfavourable outwardly — "It may be that you dislike a thing that is good for you" (2:216). Ibn Kathir's own reading of ayah 18 makes the same point from the other end: it was *on account of the peace treaty* that so much good followed.

**Keep the honour where Allah put it.** The pledge is honoured; the tree was cut down. Sayyidnā ʿUmar's action shows how seriously the early community guarded the boundary between remembering a blessing and venerating an object.

**Guard your tongue about the Companions.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's conclusion follows directly from ayah 18: Allah announced His pleasure with these people, so investigating their shortcomings and making it a subject of debate is at odds with the declaration of the verse itself.

**Honour what you have pledged.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the purpose of the announcement is to compliment the participants *and* to emphasise the obligation of fulfilling the covenant. A pledge given to Allah — in a moment of resolve, in repentance, in a commitment to worship — is meant to be kept after the moment cools.

**Trust the encompassing when the outcome is out of reach.** What Allah names in ayah 21 as not yet within your power He describes in the same sentence as already encircled by Him. And Ibn Kathir's note stands alongside it: Allah provides for those who have taqwā from resources they could never imagine.

passages.title: No battle at Hudaybiyah: Allah restrained both hands
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat look back at a battle that never happened. At Hudaybiyah, armed men were within reach of one another on the edge of Makkah — and no fighting took place. Allah tells the believers three things about that non-event: that had the disbelievers fought, they would have turned and fled (22); that this is His unchanging way (23); and that the reason no blood was shed is that He Himself withheld both sets of hands — theirs from you, and yours from them (24). What holds the passage together is a single claim: the quiet of that day was Allah's doing, and it was a favour.

## Ayah 22: the battle that was never fought

"And if those who disbelieve fight against you, they certainly would have turned their backs; then they would have found neither a protector nor a helper."

This is a sentence about something that did not happen. The Arabic sets up a condition contrary to fact — *law qātalakum*, "had they fought you" — and then answers it with the certainty of a report: they *would have* turned their backs.

Ibn Kathir reads it as glad tidings delivered to Allah's believing servants: had the idolaters fought them, Allah would have given victory to His Messenger ﷺ and His faithful servants. The army of the disbelievers would have been defeated, and would have deserted the battlefield and fled.

Then comes the clause that explains everything: **"they would have found neither a protector nor a helper."** Ibn Kathir renders it as finding no helper and no supporter at all — and he gives the reason plainly: **because they were fighting Allah, His Messenger ﷺ, and His Faithful Party.** That is the whole of it. Numbers, weapons and alliances count for nothing when the party being opposed is Allah Himself; there is simply no ally available on that side of the line.

Notice the direction of the reassurance. The Companions came away from Hudaybiyah without a fight and without entering Makkah. This ayah tells them what would have happened if it had gone the other way — that the day they walked away from was a day Allah would have decided in their favour.

## Ayah 23: Allah's unchanging way

"That has been the way of Allah already with those who passed away before. And you will not find any change in the way of Allah."

Ibn Kathir explains this as **the way Allah deals with His creation: whenever faith and disbelief meet at any distinguishing juncture, Allah gives victory to faith over disbelief, raises truth high, and destroys falsehood.**

His example is Badr. There, Ibn Kathir says, Allah helped His loyal faithful supporters and they defeated His idolater enemies, even though the Muslims were few in number and lightly armed while the idolaters were large in number and heavily armed. Badr had already displayed the pattern; ayah 22's "what would have happened" is that same pattern applied to a confrontation that never got started.

The closing clause carries as much weight as the rule itself: "you will not find any change in the way of Allah." This is not a description of one generation's good fortune but a fixed way of dealing that does not get substituted for another — as reliable in the reader's century as it was in the Companions'.

## Ayah 24: He held back both hands

"And He it is Who has withheld their hands from you and your hands from them in the midst of Makkah, after He had made you victors over them. And Allah is Ever the All-Seer of what you do."

Two hands, restrained in one breath — and the second half is the surprising half. It would have been enough to say that Allah stopped the enemy's hands; that is a straightforward rescue. But the ayah also says Allah stopped the believers' own hands, and Ibn Kathir counts the whole of it among Allah's favours to His faithful servants.

Ibn Kathir explains: Allah restrained the hands of the idolaters, and thereby no harm touched the Muslims from them; and Allah restrained the hands of the believers, so that they did not fight the idolaters near al-Masjid al-Haram. Rather — and this is the heart of his comment — **Allah saved both parties from battle and brought forth a peace treaty that produced good results for the believers**, in addition to earning them the good end in this life and in the Hereafter.

So the passage asks the believer to read a hand held back as a gift rather than a frustration. What looked on the day like an opportunity withdrawn was, in Ibn Kathir's reading, a rescue of both sides and a treaty whose fruit came later.

**"After He had made you victors over them."** This phrase is not abstract. Two incidents from that day sit behind it in the commentary.

**The seventy who were released.** Ibn Kathir recalls a narration from Salamah ibn al-Akwa': when the Muslims brought forward those seventy idolater prisoners, they tied them and paraded them before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who looked at them and said, *"Release them, so that they earn the burden of starting hostilities and its infamy."* Ibn Kathir says this ayah was then sent down about that incident. (The commentary recalls this narration without naming the collection it comes from, so we pass on the teaching without attaching a source to it.)

**The eighty from at-Tan'im.** Imam Ahmad recorded that Anas ibn Malik said: "On the day of Hudaybiyyah, eighty armed men from Makkah went down the valley coming from Mount at-Tan'im to ambush the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Messenger ﷺ invoked Allah against them, and they were taken prisoners." 'Affan added that the Messenger ﷺ pardoned them, and that this ayah was later revealed. Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim, Abu Dawud in his *Sunan*, and at-Tirmidhi and an-Nasa'i in the Tafsir sections of their *Sunan*, collected this hadith.

Put the two together and "after He had made you victors over them" becomes concrete: men who came armed were taken, and then let go. That release is what "your hands from them" looked like in practice. And the reason the Prophet ﷺ gave for it — that the burden of beginning hostilities, and its infamy, should rest on them — is instruction in how to handle a provocation.

**"In the midst of Makkah."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the Arabic word *baṭn*, which literally means "belly," and which, when used of a city, refers to its centre. Here, it says, the word is applied to Hudaybiyah because of its close proximity to Makkah — and this supports the view of the Hanafi school (one of the established schools of Islamic law) that some parts of Hudaybiyah are included within the Ḥaram, the sacred precinct around Makkah. That commentary refers the reader to its own discussion at 2:196 for the details.

**"And Allah is Ever the All-Seer of what you do."** The passage closes on Allah's seeing. The restraint of that day was not unobserved: the One who withheld the hands is the same One who sees what His servants do.

## Living it

- **Count restraint as help.** Ayah 24 places Allah's holding back of *your* hand among His favours. On Ibn Kathir's reading, both parties were saved from battle and a treaty came out of it that produced good results for the believers — and a good end in this life and the Hereafter.
- **Do not measure a confrontation by the numbers.** Ibn Kathir's rule on ayah 23, illustrated at Badr, is that when faith and disbelief meet at a decisive juncture Allah raises the truth high — while the other side, for all its apparent strength, finds neither protector nor helper.
- **Know who is actually being opposed.** The reason the idolaters would have found no ally is the reason Ibn Kathir names: they were fighting Allah, His Messenger ﷺ, and His Faithful Party.
- **Let the wrong start belong to the other party.** The words spoken over the prisoners — release them, so that the burden of beginning hostilities and its infamy is theirs — are a standing lesson in how a believer answers provocation.
- **Remember that the way does not change.** "You will not find any change in the way of Allah" is stated as a permanent fact about how Allah deals with His creation, not as a report about one generation.

passages.title: Barred from the Sacred Mosque; zeal against serenity
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat explain *why* Allah held the Muslims back from fighting at Al-Hudaybiyyah — and what He put into their hearts instead. Ayah 25 names the crime of Quraysh and then reveals the hidden reason the sword stayed sheathed; ayah 26 contrasts two things placed in two sets of hearts: the pride and haughtiness the disbelievers put in theirs, and the tranquillity Allah sent down upon His Messenger ﷺ and the believers. Read together, they are a study in the difference between zeal and serenity.

## The scene: a peaceful pilgrimage turned away

Ibn Kathir gathers the story from a long narration Al-Bukhari records in his *Sahih* in the Book of Conditions, from Al-Miswar bin Makhramah and Marwan bin Al-Hakam, each narrating and attesting to the truthfulness of the other.

The Prophet ﷺ set out at the time of Al-Hudaybiyyah with several hundred of his Companions. At Dhul-Hulayfah he had the sacrificial animals garlanded and marked and entered the state of ihram for 'Umrah — the unmistakable dress of a pilgrim, not an army. He had sent several men of the tribe of Khuza'ah ahead to gather news, and at a village called Al-Ashtat his advance regiment came back with the report that Quraysh had gathered their forces against him — including the Al-Ahabish tribes, allies who had joined Quraysh's muster — "intent on fighting you, stopping you, and preventing you."

He ﷺ consulted his Companions: should they strike at the families of those blocking the House? Abu Bakr answered, "You only intended to visit the House, not to kill anyone or start a war. Therefore, head towards the House and whoever stands in our way, then we will fight him." The Prophet ﷺ said, "Go forth, in the Name of Allah, the Exalted."

Then came the sign. When he reached the mountain pass through which he could reach them, his she-camel Al-Qaswa' sat down and would not rise, however hard the people tried. They said she had turned stubborn. He ﷺ said: **"Al-Qaswa' has not become stubborn, for stubbornness is not her habit, but she was stopped by Him Who stopped the elephant."** The One who had once stopped the elephant was now stopping the believers themselves — for their own good. And immediately he ﷺ swore: "By the Name of Him in Whose Hands is my soul, if they ask me anything which will respect the ordinances of Allah, the Exalted, I will grant it to them." That oath is the key to everything that followed; as Az-Zuhri says in the narration, the Prophet ﷺ accepted all those things precisely because he had already said he would accept everything they demanded, so long as it respected the ordinance of Allah.

## Ayah 25: the charge sheet

"**They are those who disbelieved and hindered you from Al-Masjid Al-Haram and detained the sacrificial animals, from reaching their place of sacrifice.**"

Ibn Kathir explains that these are the Arab idolators of Quraysh and their allies who extended help to them against His Messenger ﷺ. On "hindered you from Al-Masjid Al-Haram" he adds a stinging clause: *even though you are its people and more worthy of being responsible for it.* The believers were not intruders at the Sacred Mosque; they were the ones who truly honoured it, and they were the ones locked out.

The second charge concerns the *hady* — the sacrificial animals. Ibn Kathir says they prevented them, "because of transgression and stubbornness," from reaching the place where they would be slaughtered. There were seventy sacrificial camels designated for sacrifice. Imam Ahmad records from 'Abdullah bin 'Abbas that on the day of Hudaybiyyah the Messenger of Allah ﷺ slaughtered seventy sacrificial camels, including a camel that had belonged to Abu Jahl — and that when this camel was prevented from coming to the House, she cried just as she would cry when seeing her offspring. Even the animal felt the wrongness of being turned away.

Note what this establishes: Quraysh were in the wrong on every count. The believers' anger was not misplaced. Which makes the next half of the ayah far more striking.

## The hidden Muslims of Makkah

"**Had there not been believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you may kill them and on whose account a sin would have been committed by you without knowledge...**"

Ibn Kathir unpacks the meaning: there were faithful believers, men and women, living among the Makkans, *hiding their faith for fear for their safety from the pagans* — believers about whom the Muslim army had no knowledge, and whom they might have tried to kill. Had they not been there, Allah says in effect, "We would have given you authority over the Makkans and you would have killed them to the brink of extermination." The restraint at Hudaybiyyah was not weakness in the Muslim position. It was protection of a hidden minority whom the Muslim army could not tell apart from the enemy.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws this out from the word **تَزَيَّلُوا (tazayyalū)** in "if they had been apart, We would surely have punished those of them who disbelieved with a painful torment." Lexically *tazayyul* denotes separation. The sense: had the Muslims detained in Makkah been separate and distinct from the unbelievers, the Muslims coming from Madinah would have been able to save them in case of war, and Allah would have had the disbelievers punished then and there, because that was what their attitude demanded. But Makkan society at that time was a mixed society: helpless Muslim men and women living together with non-Muslims, indistinguishable from them. Had fighting broken out, there would have been no way to save them. **Therefore Allah averted the war.**

### The word *maʿarrah*

The ayah says such a killing would have brought upon the believers a **مَعَرَّة (maʿarrah)**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the authorities on lexicology differ: some say it connotes *sin*, others *harm*, others *shame* or *embarrassment* — and in this context the last meaning appears to be the apt one. Ibn Kathir renders the phrase as an evil and erroneous act committed without knowledge. Imam Qurtubi, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites him, resolves the tension: if a Muslim unknowingly kills another Muslim, it is not a sin or crime — it is *qatl khaṭaʾ*, accidental killing, to which the laws of *diyah* (blood-money) apply — but it is certainly a source of shame, embarrassment and regret.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws a fine conclusion. Allah protected the noble Companions against this as well. This shows that they are not infallible as the prophets of Allah are; rather Allah, in general terms, safeguarded them in a natural way against mistakes that would have been a cause of embarrassment and reproach to them. Had that battle happened, the Muslim army would have unwittingly killed their own Muslim brethren in faith — causing great injury to their own cause, and incurring obloquy for themselves.

### Mercy as the reason

"**...that Allah might bring into His mercy whom He wills.**"

Ibn Kathir: Allah might delay the punishment of the pagans of Makkah to save the believers who lived among them, *and* so that many of the idolators might themselves embrace Islam. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same — Allah infused patience into the Muslims on this occasion to avoid war, because He knew that many people in the future would embrace Islam and have His mercy showered on them, and that the nucleus of Muslims detained in Makkah would also receive a large share of it.

This is the deepest lesson of ayah 25. What looked to the Companions like a humiliating retreat was in reality a door held open — for hidden believers who would otherwise have died, and for future Muslims who at that moment were still enemies. The mercy that spared Quraysh that day was aimed at people who had not yet believed.

## Ayah 26: two hearts, two contents

"**When those who disbelieve had put in their hearts pride and haughtiness — the pride and haughtiness of the time of ignorance.**"

The Arabic word rendered here as "pride and haughtiness" is **حَمِيَّة (ḥamiyyah)**, and the ayah qualifies it as **ḥamiyyat al-jāhiliyyah** — the ḥamiyyah of *jāhiliyyah*, the time of ignorance before Islam. Ibn Kathir identifies exactly which moment the ayah is pointing at: when they refused to write in the treaty document *"In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful,"* and *"These are the terms agreed on by Muhammad, Allah's Messenger."* At the end of that same long narration the definition is given again: their pride and haughtiness was that they did not confess that Muhammad ﷺ was the Prophet of Allah, refused to write *"In the Name of Allah, Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim,"* and prevented Muslims from visiting the Ka'bah.

The scene itself is preserved. Suhayl bin 'Amr came to negotiate. The Prophet ﷺ called 'Ali bin Abi Talib and told him to write "In the Name of Allah, Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim." Suhayl objected: "As for Ar-Rahman, by Allah, I do not know what it means. So write: By Your Name, O Allah, as you used to write previously." The Muslims said, "By Allah, we will not write except: By the Name of Allah, Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Write: *In Your Name, O Allah*." Then, over "Muhammad, Allah's Messenger," Suhayl said: "By Allah, if we knew that you are Allah's Messenger, we would not prevent you from visiting the Ka'bah, and would not fight with you. So, write: Muhammad bin 'Abdullah." The Prophet ﷺ replied, **"By Allah! I am the Messenger of Allah even if your people do not believe me. Write: Muhammad bin 'Abdullah."**

Imam Ahmad records a narration from Ibn 'Abbas in which he ﷺ said to 'Ali, "Erase it. O Allah! You know that I am Your Messenger" — and Ibn 'Abbas used this as an argument against Al-Haruriyyah, a group who had rebelled and set up a separate camp of their own: the Messenger ﷺ erased his title, and erasing his title did not mean that he was erased from being a Prophet. Ibn 'Abbas's point is worth holding on to: a man secure in what Allah knows of him does not need the enemy's parchment to confirm it. That is the exact opposite of *ḥamiyyah*.

Notice too what the ayah says about that pride: *those who disbelieved put it in their hearts.* It was their own doing, their own choice of what to fill the heart with. What filled the believers' hearts came down from elsewhere.

## The sakinah and the word of taqwa

"**Then Allah sent down His calmness and tranquillity (sakīnah) upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and made them stick to the word of Taqwa; and they were well entitled to it and worthy of it. And Allah is the All-Knower of everything.**"

Two gifts, exactly answering the two failures on the other side. Against their pride and haughtiness — *sakīnah*, the calmness and tranquillity Allah Himself sent down. Against their refusal to name Allah and His Messenger — Allah made the believers stick firmly to **kalimat at-taqwā**, the word of taqwa, of mindfulness of Allah.

What is that word? Ibn Kathir reports the explanations of the early authorities:

- **Mujahid**: it refers to sincerity.
- **'Ata' bin Abi Rabah**: "None has the right to be worshipped but Allah, alone without partners. All the dominion belongs to Him and all praise is due to Him. He is Ever Able to do everything."
- **Al-Miswar**, in the chain Yunus bin Bukayr gives from Ibn Ishaq from Az-Zuhri from 'Urwah: "*La ilaha illallah*, alone without partners."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers these into one: *kalimat at-taqwā* is the word of the pious — the Kalimah of Tawhid and Risalah, by which a person declares his faith in Allah's Oneness and in the messengership of Muhammad ﷺ. It is named the "word of piety" because this word is the foundation of piety, righteousness and right conduct.

And then the ayah's remarkable closing verdict on the Companions: **they were well entitled to it and worthy of it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that with this, Allah exposed and unmasked those people who accused them of infidelity and hypocrisy. Allah asserts that the noble Companions are more worthy of the word of Islam and better entitled to it, and thus made them adhere to it firmly — whereas the wretched, evil-minded refuse to acknowledge their value and entitlement.

## What the sakinah looked like on the ground

It is important not to imagine *sakīnah* as an absence of feeling. The narrations show the Companions in real anguish, and the tranquillity was what carried them *through* it, not around it.

In the Book of Conditions narration, 'Umar bin Al-Khattab came to the Prophet ﷺ: "Aren't you truly the Messenger of Allah?" — "Yes, indeed." — "Isn't our cause just and the cause of the enemy unjust?" — "Yes." — "Then why should we be humble in our religion?" He ﷺ answered: **"I am Allah's Messenger and I do not disobey Him, and He will make me victorious."** 'Umar pressed: had he not told them they would perform Tawaf? He ﷺ said: "Yes, but did I tell you that we would visit the Ka'bah *this year*? ... So you will visit it and perform Tawaf around it." 'Umar then took the same questions to Abu Bakr and received the same answers, with the addition: "Adhere to him for, by Allah, he is on the right path." Az-Zuhri reports 'Umar saying afterwards, "I performed many good deeds as expiation for the improper questions I asked them."

Then came Abu Jandal — Suhayl's own son, Abu Jandal bin Suhayl bin 'Amr, coming from the valley of Makkah staggering in his chains and falling down among the Muslims, having been tortured severely for the cause of Allah, only to be claimed back under a clause not yet even written. "O Muslims! Will I be returned to the idolators although I have come as a Muslim? Don't you see how much I have suffered?"

And when the writing of the treaty was concluded, the Prophet ﷺ said to his Companions, "Get up and slaughter your sacrifices and have your heads shaved." By Allah, none of them got up. He repeated the order three times. He then left them and went in to Umm Salamah, who advised him: go out, do not say a word to anybody, slaughter your own sacrifice and call your barber. He ﷺ went out and did not talk to anyone until he did exactly that — and seeing it, the Companions got up, slaughtered their sacrifices, and started shaving one another's heads, in so much of a rush and sadness that there was a danger of killing each other.

That is what *sakīnah* looked like: hearts breaking, and still holding. Zeal would have drawn the sword; serenity kept the hand still and let Allah's promise arrive on Allah's schedule.

## Living it

There is a second, entirely separate hadith that Ibn Kathir brings here. Al-Bukhari narrated in the Book of Tafsir that Habib bin Abi Thabit said he went to Abu Wa'il, who related: they were at Siffin — long after Hudaybiyyah, when Muslims were in dispute with one another — and Sahl bin Hunayf stood up and said: **"Do not feel certain in the reliability of your own opinions!"** On the day of Hudaybiyyah, he said, the day the treaty of peace was signed between the Prophet ﷺ and the idolators, had they found a chance to fight, they would have done so. In another wording of the same hadith: "O people! Accuse sheer opinion of being imperfect! On the day Abu Jandal came, I saw myself willing to reject the command of Allah's Messenger ﷺ, had I had the chance."

Sahl then recounted, in this narration, his own version of 'Umar's questioning: 'Umar came and said, "Are we not on the true cause and theirs is the false cause? Are not our killed in Paradise and theirs in the Fire?" He ﷺ said, "Yes." 'Umar said, "Why then should we be humble with regards to the cause of our religion?" The Prophet ﷺ said, **"O son of Al-Khattab! I am Allah's Messenger and He will never abandon me."** 'Umar left feeling angry and went to Abu Bakr with the same question, and Abu Bakr said, **"O son of Al-Khattab! He is Allah's Messenger and Allah will never abandon him."** Surat Al-Fath was later revealed. (Ibn Kathir notes that Al-Bukhari collected this hadith in several other parts of his *Sahih*, as did Muslim and An-Nasa'i, through various chains from Abu Wa'il, Sufyan bin Salamah, from Sahl bin Hunayf.)

That is the passage's most practical gift. A believer can be entirely right about the facts — the cause just, the enemy unjust, the exclusion from the Sacred Mosque a genuine outrage — and still be wrong about what should be done, because he cannot see the hidden believers in the enemy's city, or the mercy Allah intends for people who are still his opponents.

So the passage asks three things. **Distrust your own certainty** when it runs against the guidance you have been given; that is precisely what Sahl bin Hunayf told the disputing Muslims at Siffin, and what 'Umar spent good deeds in expiation for. **Recognise your zeal for what it is** — ask whether what fills your heart in a confrontation is taqwa or *ḥamiyyah*, the pride and haughtiness of the time of ignorance; the disbelievers of Quraysh forfeited everything by clinging to their pride over a line of writing. And **hold to the word of taqwa** — the Kalimah that is the foundation of piety, righteousness and right conduct — trusting, as Abu Bakr told 'Umar, that Allah will never abandon His Messenger, and that the Tawaf denied this year is only postponed, not cancelled: "So you will visit it and perform Tawaf around it."

passages.title: The vision fulfilled and the Messenger named
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close Sūrat al-Fatḥ by answering the question still hanging over the believers after Ḥudaybiyah: *the Prophet ﷺ saw a dream of entering Makkah — so why did we turn back?* Allah answers on three widening levels: the vision will come true (ayah 27), the mission it belongs to will prevail over every religion (ayah 28), and the men who obeyed are described — in the earlier Books as well as this one (ayah 29).

## The dream, and the year it did not happen

Ibn Kathir gives the background. In a dream, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw himself entering Makkah and performing ṭawāf — circling the Kaʿbah — and told his Companions in Madinah. So when they set out in the year of Ḥudaybiyah, **none of them doubted the vision would come true that year**.

Then it did not. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb asked: "Haven't you told us that we will go to the House and perform ṭawāf around it?" The Prophet ﷺ answered, "Yes. Have I told you that you will go to it *this year*?" ʿUmar said, "No." He ﷺ said, "Then you will go to it and perform ṭawāf around it." Ibn Kathir notes ʿUmar received the same answer from Abu Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq, letter for letter.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the pain was so sharp. Their determination to perform ʿumrah — the lesser pilgrimage, which may be made at any time of year — rested on that vision, and a prophetic vision is itself a kind of revelation. When everything appeared to happen contrary to it, some began to wonder whether the vision had failed, while the disbelievers and hypocrites taunted the believers that their Prophet's ﷺ dream had not been translated into reality. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports (transmitted by Baihaqi and others from Mujahid) that **these verses were revealed at exactly that moment**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurṭubī, records Abu Bakr's reasoning: no date or year was specified in the vision, so if it did not happen now, it will happen at some other time.

## "Allah has made the vision come true" — a grammar of certainty

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the key word. **Ṣidq** (truth) is the opposite of **kidhb** (falsehood), and both normally describe *statements*. But ṣidq is sometimes used of *actions*, where it means bringing something into actual realisation — as in "men who were true to their covenant with Allah" (33:23). Here *ṣadaqa* takes two objects: "His Messenger" and "the vision." Allah did not merely *say* the vision was true; He **made it come true**.

Two grammatical choices press the certainty home:

- **Past tense for a future event.** "Allah has made true" is put in the past perfect, though the entry had not yet happened — used, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, precisely because the occurrence is certain.
- **The energetic form.** *La-tadkhulunna*, "you will most definitely enter," stacks two intensifiers: the corroborative *lā* ("certainly") and the doubled energetic *nūn* ("most definitely").

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the Companions in their enthusiasm resolved to set out *that very year*, and the Prophet ﷺ concurred; there was much divine wisdom in that, which became manifest at Ḥudaybiyah.

## Why Allah says "if Allah wills"

Allah attaches *in shāʼ Allāh* to His own promise. Qurṭubī, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, notes the puzzle: Allah is fully aware of His own will and had no need of the phrase. He used it anyway — **to teach the Messenger ﷺ and the people the importance of saying "in shāʼ Allāh" about future work**. Ibn Kathir comments that He willed it, so the matter shall certainly occur.

## Shaved heads and shortened hair

*Muḥalliqīna ruʼūsakum wa muqaṣṣirīn* — some with heads shaved, some with hair cut short. Ibn Kathir cites the Two Ṣaḥīḥs: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "O Allah! Be merciful to those who have their head shaved." The people said, "O Allah's Messenger! And those who get their hair cut short." He repeated the first supplication. They asked again; he repeated it again. Only the third or fourth time did he ﷺ add, "**And to those who get their hair cut short.**" A quiet ranking — mercy invoked for both, one asked for first and repeatedly.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records from Bukhari that the missed ʿumrah was performed the following year — known as **ʿUmrat al-Qaḍāʼ**, the "ʿumrah of the fulfilled promise." Then *lā takhāfūn*, "having no fear": Ibn Kathir says they would be safe when they entered Makkah, and that this came about in the ʿumrah of the seventh year of Hijrah.

## "He knew what you did not know"

Ibn Kathir reads this as mercy: Allah knew the benefit and goodness in turning them away from Makkah that year, and before the promised entry granted a **near victory**, which he identifies as the treaty of peace itself.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports both readings of that near victory:

- **Khaybar.** Here *dūna dhālik* means "before the fulfilment of the vision": Allah willed that the Muslims first conquer Khaybar and become a powerful force in material resources, so they could then perform ʿumrah peacefully.
- **Ḥudaybiyah itself.** Others hold it is the treaty, because it opened the gate to the victory of Makkah and every victory after — and eventually all the Companions acknowledged it as the greatest of all victories.

Muhammad Taqi Usmani makes this concrete. The Jews of Khaybar always conspired with the disbelievers of Makkah, so the Prophet ﷺ was encircled — Makkans to the south, Khaybar to the north — and battle with either entailed danger from behind. **The treaty made the south safe, and only then could Khaybar be taken without fear from their back.**

Ibn Kathir traces what followed: from Ḥudaybiyah in Dhul-Qaʿdah of the sixth year the Prophet ﷺ returned to Madinah, and in Ṣafar marched on Khaybar, which Allah opened for him partly by force and partly by its people surrendering, and he ﷺ divided it **among those who had attended Ḥudaybiyah with him**.

## The year the dream came true

In Dhul-Qaʿdah of the seventh year of Hijrah the Prophet ﷺ went to Makkah for ʿumrah with those who had been with him at Ḥudaybiyah, resuming iḥrām from Dhul-Ḥulayfah. Nearing Marr aẓ-Ẓahrān he sent Muḥammad ibn Maslamah ahead with the horses and weapons; the idolaters, seeing this advance regiment, were overwhelmed with fear that he had betrayed the treaty. So he ﷺ sent the weaponry to the valley of Yaʼjaj, and went on with the swords resting in their sheaths, as the treaty stipulated. When Quraysh sent Mikraz ibn Ḥafṣ, who said, "O Muhammad! We never knew you to be one who betrays his promises," the Prophet ﷺ explained where he had sent it. Mikraz answered: "**This is the way we knew you to be, trustworthy and keeping to your promises.**"

The Prophet ﷺ entered reciting the talbiyah, riding his camel al-Qaṣwāʼ — the same camel he had ridden on the day of Ḥudaybiyah — with ʿAbdullah ibn Rawāḥah holding the bridle and repeating a poem, including the line that today "we shall impose on you the fulfillment of its interpretation, just as we fought with you to accept its revelation."

Ibn Kathir preserves here the origin of **ramal**, the brisk walk in ṭawāf. Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbās — and the Two Ṣaḥīḥs also recorded it — that the fever of Yathrib had weakened the Muslims, and the idolaters circulated the news that a people weakened by that fever were coming, then sat in the area close to al-Ḥijr to watch. Allah conveyed to His Prophet ﷺ what they said, so he ordered his Companions to do ramal in the first three rounds so the idolaters would witness their strength, and to walk normally between the two corners, where the idolaters could not see them — and he did not order ramal in all the rounds, **out of pity for them**. The idolaters commented: "Are these the people whom you claimed were weakened by the fever. They are stronger than so-and-so!"

Al-Bukhari records from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar that when he ﷺ had stayed three days, the idolaters ordered him to depart, as the treaty allowed — and he ﷺ departed. The vision was fulfilled, one year late.

## Ayah 28: the mission behind the moment

Ibn Kathir reads the two terms as the two factors of the Islamic Sharīʿah: **guidance** is beneficial knowledge, **the religion of truth** is righteous deeds — so the news and creed this religion conveys are true and its commandments are just. "Superior to all religions" he takes at full breadth: all the religions of the people of the earth, Arabs and non-Arabs alike. And Allah suffices as Witness that Muhammad is His Messenger ﷺ and that He will grant him victory.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places the ayah structurally: the sūrah has promised conquests and spoils, named the merits of the participants of Ḥudaybiyah and of all the Companions, and given glad tidings — and since all of it came through obeying the Messenger ﷺ, the closing ayat press that obedience home, denounce those who reject his messengership, and allay the suspicions of Muslims still dissatisfied with the treaty. The ayah makes **a very bold prophecy**: not only would Islam prevail in Arabia, it would eventually triumph over all other religions — declared by a man just turned back from his own city.

## Ayah 29: the name they erased

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something exquisite. The Qurʼan's general style is not to call the Prophet ﷺ by his personal name but by an attributive name — *yā ayyuha'n-Nabiyy*, *yā ayyuha'r-Rasūl* — unlike other prophets, addressed by their personal names: *yā Ibrāhīm*, *yā Mūsā*. He ﷺ is addressed by his personal name "Muhammad" only four times in the entire Qurʼan, and only where there is a special reason.

The reason here is Ḥudaybiyah. As the treaty was being written the pagan Quraysh objected to the attributive name being used with the personal name; they **wiped off "Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah"** and insisted on "Muhammad son of ʿAbdullah," and by Allah's command the Messenger ﷺ accepted it. So Allah, on this very occasion, especially attached *rasūl Allāh* to the personal name in His Last Book — to be written and recited like that until the Day of Judgement. What was rubbed off a parchment was engraved into revelation. Ibn Kathir adds that Allah here declares without doubt that Muhammad ﷺ is truly His Messenger, and this quality includes every beautiful description.

## The portrait of the Companions

Ibn Kathir pairs "severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves" with 5:54 — "humble towards the believers, stern towards the disbelievers" — and draws it concretely: angry without smiling before the disbeliever, smiling before his believing brother. He cites a hadith collected in the Ṣaḥīḥ, in which the Prophet ﷺ said: "The parable of the believers in their kindness and mercy for each other is that of the body: when one of its organs falls ill, the rest of the body responds with fever and sleeplessness."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān guards this against misuse. "Severe against the disbelievers" does **not** imply they were never tender towards any non-believer; it means that where Allah and His Messenger ﷺ enjoined firmness they simply complied, without taking into account relations of kinship or friendship. That is why the quality is listed first: nothing they practised — friendship or enmity, love or hatred — was for selfish reasons; everything was for the sake of Allah and His Messenger. In a hadith recorded by Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ said: "He who loves for the sake of Allah and hates for the sake of Allah has attained the highest degree of faith." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then recalls that Allah does not forbid you from doing good and dealing justly with those who did not fight you on account of faith and did not expel you from your homes (60:8), and notes a large number of incidents where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Companions displayed kindness to the helpless and needy unbelievers.

Being preoccupied with bowing and prostrating is, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's framing, the mark of perfection **in deeds** as the first quality was the mark of perfection **in faith**, because ṣalāh is the most meritorious of all good deeds. Ibn Kathir stresses the sincerity: they are sincere to Allah in the prayer, awaiting His generous reward alone — and "the greatest bliss is the acceptance by Allah" (9:72).

**The mark on their faces.** Ibn Kathir gathers the early views: Ibn ʿAbbās (as reported from him by ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah) said it refers to graceful appearance; Mujahid and several others explained it as humbleness and reverence. He cites Imam Ahmad from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbās — a hadith Abu Dawud also collected — that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Verily, good conduct, graceful appearance and moderation are one part out of twenty-five parts of prophethood." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that the mark does not necessarily refer to a physical sign on the forehead, but to the light reflected naturally on the faces of the devout from humility and meekness — particularly one of the effects of offering tahajjud, the night prayer, regularly. Ḥasan al-Baṣrī held that the "features" refer to the light the faces of those who pray will emit on the Day of Judgement.

## The two Books, and the growing crop

Ibn Kathir explains the image piece by piece: *shaṭʼah* is the shoot or branch; *fa-āzarahu*, it is made able to stand on its own; *fa-staghlaẓa*, it becomes thick and long; then it stands straight on its stem, delighting the sowers. Such is the parable of the Companions of Allah's Messenger ﷺ — they gave the Messenger ﷺ aid, support and victory, just as the shoot hardens the plant. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces that growth historically: at one time, besides the Prophet ﷺ, there were only three Muslims — Abu Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq among men, Khadījah among women, ʿAlī among children — and the Companions who performed the Farewell Pilgrimage with him ﷺ are said to have numbered about 150,000.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a question over where the sentence pauses, and so which description belongs to which Book; since the present-day Torah and Gospel have been subjected to alterations, the true import cannot be determined with certainty, though **most commentators** prefer the reading in which the light of the faces is the Torah's description and the crop is the Injīl's. Qatādah quotes the Injīl: "Such a people will emerge who will grow like a crop; they will enjoin good works and forbid evil works."

## The promise, and how a believer speaks of them

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stops on one small word in "those of them who believe." The *min* in *minhum* is, by consensus of Qurʼanic scholarly opinion, **explicative** (*min li'l-bayān*), not partitive: it clarifies — as in "refrain from the filth of the idols" (22:30). So the promise of forgiveness and a mighty reward covers them all without exception; the partitive reading is completely incompatible with the context — for Allah announced His pleasure with the believers who pledged allegiance under the tree (ayah 18), and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, quoting this verse in the introduction to his *Istīʿāb*, wrote: "He with whom Allah is pleased, He will never be displeased with him."

Ibn Kathir reports that Imam Malik, relying on "that He may enrage the disbelievers with them," stated that the Rawāfiḍ are disbelievers because they hate the Companions: "he who is enraged by the Companions is a disbeliever." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports a different incident: Abu ʿUrwah az-Zubayrī said that when a man uttered a belittling statement against the Companions in Imam Malik's gathering, the Imam recited this entire ayah and said the warning applies to anyone who belittles them — and notes that **there the Imam did not say such a person becomes a disbeliever**, only that his conduct will be like that of the unbelievers.

Both agree on the prohibition of insulting them. Ibn Kathir cites Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not abuse my Companions, for by the One in Whose Hand is my soul! If one of you spends the amount of Uḥud in gold, that amount will never reach the level of one of them spending a *mudd*, or half of it" — a *mudd* being a small dry measure. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a hadith recorded in Tirmidhi on the authority of ʿAbdullah ibn Mughaffal in which the Prophet ﷺ said: "Fear Allah, fear Allah regarding my Companions! Do not make them a target of your criticism after me… he who injures them has injured me."

Ibn Kathir closes with balance: all those who follow the guidance of the Companions will be similar to them — yet the Companions have the better virtue, the obvious lead and a perfection in character on account of which none in this Ummah will be able to attain their level.

## Living it

**Trust the timing, not your reading of it.** The Companions had a true vision from a true Prophet ﷺ and still misread *when*. What looked like failure was a flank being cleared.

**Say "in shāʼ Allāh" and mean it.** Allah attached it to His own certain promise so that you would attach it to your uncertain ones.

**Guard your tongue about the Companions — and imitate them.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the Qurʼan portrays them at such length: the Prophet ﷺ is the Final Messenger; he left behind the Book of Allah *and* the paradigm of his Companions, with specific injunctions to emulate their pattern of life. Ayah 29 is that template: firmness where Allah requires it, mercy inside the community, and a life so shaped by prayer that it shows.
